papers.title: Differential and Cooperative Immunomodulation by Saponin Adjuvants QS-21 and QS-7 in Human THP-1 Macrophages
papers.abstract: QS-21, a triterpene glycoside saponin derived from Quillaja saponaria, is a potent immunostimulatory adjuvant incorporated in several FDA-approved vaccines. QS-7, a structurally related saponin fraction, has been reported to retain immunomodulatory activity with reduced hemolytic toxicity; however, its lower natural abundance has limited its systematic immunological characterization. To address this gap, we systematically compare responses to QS-21 and QS-7 in the THP-1 human macrophage model to resolve their distinct and cooperative contributions to antigen presenting cell (APC) activation. Following cytotoxicity profiling to establish safe and biologically relevant dosing, flow cytometry, proteomics, and transcriptomics were used to delineate the immunological programs engaged by each saponin alone and in combination. QS-7 alone induced minimal upregulation of cell surface activation markers and did not elicit a significant transcriptional signature, yet it drove dose-dependent secretion of a broad panel of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, revealing a dissociation between these two arms of macrophage activation. Strikingly, co-administration of QS-7 with QS-21 substantially potentiated macrophage activation across all parameters tested, amplifying surface marker upregulation, broadening cytokine and chemokine output to include IL-12p70 and IFN-γ, and markedly expanding the pro-inflammatory transcriptional and pathway landscape induced by QS-21, while concurrently suppressing counter-regulatory lipid-sensing pathways (PPAR, RAR, FXR/RXR) that constrain inflammatory output. Collectively, these findings establish QS-7 not merely as an attenuated analog of QS-21, but as a functionally distinct immunomodulator that recalibrates both the magnitude and regulatory tone of QS-21-driven macrophage activation. These findings show that structurally distinct saponins elicit distinct and complementary macrophage responses, providing a foundation for structure-function studies. Together with synthetic biology and data-driven design, this knowledge can guide the development of new-to-nature saponin adjuvants.

papers.title: Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase bifunctionally catalyzes ring formation involving sequential terminal carbon oxidation for pyrrolizidinone alkaloid biosynthesis.
papers.abstract: The Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase UcsF plays a key role in the early biosynthesis of UCS1025A, an antibacterial and antitumor pyrrolizidinone alkaloid, by participating in the formation of its core ring scaffold. UcsF catalyzes sequential oxidation of the terminal C5 of L-isoleucine, ultimately generating a five-membered ring product, (2S,3S)-3,4-dihydro-3-methyl-2H-pyrrole-2-carboxylic acid. This catalytic process is vital in the construction of natural product skeletons and synthetic biology. However, the molecular basis of UcsF and its unique two-step catalytic mechanism remain poorly understood. We characterized the catalytic function of UcsF, determined its crystal structure and combined molecular docking and MD simulations to reveal the molecular basis for substrate recognition, and employed quantum chemical calculations on reaction-state models to investigate plausible reaction pathways underlying the sequential oxidation. UcsF exhibits catalytic activity toward 2-amino carboxylic acid substrates. The crystal structure of UcsF features a unique open active pocket, with substrate binding defined by the collective contributions of multiple structural modules. In the catalytic reaction, the Fe(IV) = O species abstracts a hydrogen atom from the C5 position of L-isoleucine, followed by hydroxyl rebound to complete the first hydroxylation step. Combined kinetic, solvent isotope-effect, mutational, and computational analyses support a preferred Asp279'-facilitated PCET pathway for the second oxidation of 5-OH-Ile to the aldehyde product. Our study provides a molecular basis for understanding the relationship between the structure and function of Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and reveals the potential of the catalytic ability of UcsF for biosynthesis.

papers.title: Lineage-specific Emergence and Multi-layered Regulation of Limonoid Biosynthesis in Citrus.
papers.abstract: Limonoids are triterpenoid phytochemicals that contribute to delayed bitterness in citrus fruit, enhance pest resistance, and exhibit a wide range of bioactivities with nutraceutical and agrochemical potential. Despite their importance, the genetic and regulatory basis underlying limonoid biosynthesis in citrus remains poorly understood. Here, by integrating targeted metabolite profiling across 134 citrus and related accessions with comparative genomic analyses of 12 representative species from the orange subfamily (Aurantioideae), we show that the emergence of limonin, nomilin, and obacunone correlates with the citrus-specific acquisition of three downstream biosynthetic genes, CYP88A51, CYP716AC1, and limonoid furan synthase (LFS), while the upstream oxidosqualene cyclase 1 (OSC1) remains conserved across lineages. We further identify CsbHLH92 as a key transcriptional activator that directly regulates these genes, and its overexpression led to dramatic increases in limonin and nomilin levels. Moreover, CsbHLH92 activity is attenuated by CsMPK7-mediated phosphorylation, contributing to the downregulation of limonoid biosynthesis during leaf senescence, when senescing leaves are generally less preferred by insect pests. Together, our findings uncover how lineage-specific gene emergence and multi-layered regulation collectively shape the specialized metabolism of limonoids in citrus. These insights provide metabolic engineering targets for improving citrus flavor, enhancing pest resistance, and boosting the production of high-value bioactive compounds.

papers.title: Coupling environmental biosensors to inverter circuits in soil bacteria
papers.abstract: Genetic logic gates, such as inverting NOT functions, are routinely designed and optimised for a narrow set of laboratory-standard chemical inputs. This reliance limits their utility in real-world applications, where engineered chassis must navigate complex, niche-specific signals. Focusing on environmental synthetic biology, we engineered four biosensors responsive to ecologically relevant physical and chemical inputs (iron, oxygen, temperature, and light) and systematically coupled them to three repressor-based NOT logic gates (QacR, SrpR, and LitR) to generate 12 composite sensor-gate circuits. To evaluate cross-host robustness, all constructs were benchmarked in two non-model soil bacteria: Pseudomonas putida KT2440 and Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5. Our findings demonstrate that overall circuit performance is non-additive and cannot be predicted simply by summing individual sensor and gate dynamics. While standalone biosensors reliably detected their cognate inputs, concatenation across regulatory junctions introduced non-linearities, emergent dynamics, and host-dependent effects that caused several pairings to deviate unexpectedly from their predicted behaviour. Furthermore, host context directly governed logic execution: P. protegens Pf-5 exhibited superior overall circuit-processing capacity, whereas specific configurations, such as iron-responsive gates, performed better in P. putida KT2440. All 12 constructs are modularly integrated using the Standard European Vector Architecture (SEVA) format, providing a benchmarked toolkit to program complex information processing in real-world environments.

papers.title: Calcium Signaling Enhances Bostrycin Biosynthesis in Nigrospora sphaerica HCH285: Transcriptomic Insights into Metabolic Regulation
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Bostrycin, an anthraquinone secondary metabolite produced by Nigrospora sphaerica , exhibits broad-spectrum antitumor and antimicrobial activities, but its low production limits further development and application. Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) are important intracellular signaling molecules that regulate fungal physiology and secondary metabolism, but their role in bostrycin biosynthesis remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effect of exogenous Ca 2+ on bostrycin production and to elucidate the underlying molecular response using transcriptomic analysis. Methods: Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Na⁺, and K⁺ (supplemented as chloride salts) were screened for their ability to promote bostrycin production in N. sphaerica HCH285. The optimal Ca²⁺ concentration and addition time were determined by measuring bostrycin production using HPLC. Biomass accumulation, sporulation capacity, and extracellular nucleic acid and protein leakage were evaluated to characterize the physiological effects of Ca 2+ treatment.Control and Ca²⁺-treated cultures were subjected to transcriptome sequencing, followed by GO and KEGG enrichment analyses and qRT-PCR validation. Results: Among all tested metal ions, Ca 2+ showed the strongest stimulatory effect on bostrycin biosynthesis, with 4 g/L Ca 2+ producing the highest yield of bostrycin with 63.6 ± 0.31 μg/mL, representing a 2.55-fold increase over the control. Ca 2+ supplementation also significantly increased fungal biomass and sporulation capacity, suggesting that enhanced growth contributed to the elevated metabolite production. Increased extracellular nucleic acid and protein contents indicated altered cell integrity or secretion activity following Ca 2+ treatment.Transcriptomic analysis identified DEGs most significantly enriched in metabolic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation, while genes related to polyketide metabolism and ubiquinone biosynthesis were also annotated. Several genes associated with ion transport, energy metabolism, and secondary metabolite biosynthesis were significantly upregulated. Among them, wbpA, talA, cho1, and aroB were further validated by qRT-PCR, indicating that Ca²⁺ supplementation triggered broad metabolic reprogramming associated with bostrycin accumulation. Conclusions: Exogenous Ca 2+ effectively enhances bostrycin production in N. sphaerica HCH285 through coordinated physiological and transcriptional responses. Transcriptomic analysis suggests that Ca 2+ supplementation promotes energy metabolism, ion transport, and secondary metabolic processes associated with bostrycin biosynthesis. These findings provide new insights into calcium-mediated regulation of fungal secondary metabolism and offer a potential strategy for improving bostrycin production through fermentation optimization and metabolic engineering.

papers.title: Empirical optimization of dCas12a-based CRISPRi/a for pooled screening in Yarrowia lipolytica
papers.abstract: Yarrowia lipolytica is an important host for biotechnology and metabolic engineering, valued for its ability to accumulate lipids and produce a wide range of industrially relevant compounds. This creates a growing need for genome-scale tools that can accelerate the identification of genes underlying complex phenotypes. Although Cas9-based CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and activation (CRISPRa) tools are well established in Y. lipolytica, Cas12a offers a complementary platform with a T-rich PAM that can expand access to promoter regions and facilitate multiplexed regulation. Despite these advantages, Cas12a-based CRISPRi/a remains comparatively underdeveloped in Y. lipolytica, particularly for large-scale functional screening. Here, we establish and systematically benchmark dCas12a-based CRISPRi/a platforms for pooled screening in Y. lipolytica. We first compared two widely used effectors, dLbCas12a and denAsCas12a, across single-gene assays and a pooled CRISPRi library targeting nine essential or conditionally essential genes with 752 crRNAs. Both orthologs supported robust transcriptional repression, but their relative performance was crRNA- and condition-dependent, with dLbCas12a showing more consistent and stronger late-stage depletion across targets. dLbCas12a also enabled enrichment-based CRISPRi and CRISPRa screens, recovering expected drug-resistance and lipid-associated phenotypes. The broad design of the pooled library further enabled identification of crRNA features associated with CRISPRi efficacy. Highly active crRNAs were enriched near transcription start sites, with an effective targeting interval extending from approximately −260 to +50 bp. Intermediate GC content was associated with higher efficacy, while PAM identity showed a weaker but consistent effect, with TTTA and TTTT PAMs linked to stronger depletion than TTTC and TTTG PAMs. Spacer length showed the strongest association with CRISPRi efficacy, with 18-nt crRNAs consistently outperforming matched longer 20-, 23-, and 25-nt variants. Finally, we tested dHyperLbCas12a, an engineered LbCas12a variant with enhanced activity, and found that it produced substantially stronger CRISPRi and CRISPRa phenotypes than dLbCas12a. Together, these results establish Cas12a as a versatile platform for pooled CRISPRi/a screens in Y. lipolytica, identify practical crRNA prioritization rules for improved library performance, and highlight dHyperLbCas12a as a promising effector for future large-scale gain- and loss-of-function screens.

papers.title: Beyond the Primary-Secondary Dichotomy: Toward a Unified Metabolic Perspective.
papers.abstract: The distinction between primary and secondary metabolism has long provided a useful conceptual and pedagogical framework in biochemistry, particularly in plant sciences, but it increasingly fails as a literal description of how metabolites are produced and function. Pathways share precursors, cofactors, regulatory mechanisms, transport systems, and recycling routes, while metabolites conventionally assigned to different categories can contribute to growth, signaling, defense, nutrient acquisition, structure, or stress responses depending on context. Here, we review the historical origins of the primary-secondary dichotomy and synthesize biochemical, genetic, ecological, metabolomic, and systems-level evidence for a more integrated interpretation of plant metabolism. We do not argue that established terms must be abolished: they remain useful descriptors of broad tendencies in conservation, distribution, and pathway organization. Instead, we argue against treating them as fixed functional categories. We develop an operational framework in which network position, flux and resource coupling, phylogenetic distribution, spatiotemporal localization, conditional essentiality, and experimentally demonstrated function are evaluated together. We then show how this perspective changes the analysis of untargeted metabolomic data and the design of metabolic-engineering strategies. A unified metabolic perspective provides a practical way to connect plant physiology, environmental responses, and ecological interactions without replacing established terminology with a new rigid vocabulary.

papers.title: Chromosome-level genomics and cross-species enzyme screening enable high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica
papers.abstract: The diversity of enzymes supporting bakuchiol biosynthesis remains incompletely characterized, limiting the repertoire available for microbial pathway engineering. Here, we combined chromosome-level genomics, cross-species enzyme screening and metabolic engineering to establish high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica. We assembled a 471.76-Mb Psoralea corylifolia genome anchored to 11 pseudochromosomes, with a contig N50 of 40.33 Mb. Genome-guided screening and functional validation identified four prenyltransferases from P. corylifolia and Vigna radiata whose N-terminally truncated variants supported bakuchiol production in yeast. These results extend experimental evidence for bakuchiol-producing activity across legume prenyltransferase sequences and species. For PcPT6, corresponding to the previously reported PcPT07, removing 40 N-terminal amino acids increased bakuchiol production by 53% relative to the full-length enzyme. We reconstructed bakuchiol biosynthesis in Y. lipolytica and reinforced aromatic precursor synthesis to increase p-coumaric acid supply. Coordinating mevalonate pathway reinforcement with increased t40PcPT6 gene dosage further improved bakuchiol production. Following fermentation optimization, titers reached 108.29 mg/L in shake flasks and 6.03 g/L in a 7.5-L fed-batch bioreactor. These findings connect an expanded set of functional prenyltransferases with coordinated pathway engineering, enabling gram-per-liter microbial bakuchiol production.

papers.title: Cell-free protein synthesis for next-generation biomanufacturing.
papers.abstract: Chemicals with diverse molecular structures are essential to the pharmaceutical, food, and specialty chemical industries; however, their sustainable production remains challenging due to complex cellular regulation, limited metabolic flexibility, and the scalability constraints of purified enzyme-based systems. Extract-based cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) has emerged as a versatile biomanufacturing platform that enables the production of functional enzymes in vitro and provides an open, programmable environment for constructing synthetic biosynthetic systems beyond the constraints of living cells. By decoupling chemical synthesis from cellular growth, CFPS allows precise control over enzyme composition, pathway stoichiometry, and cofactor utilization, thereby improving catalytic efficiency and resource utilization. In this review, we summarize recent advances in extract-based CFPS for chemical biosynthesis and discuss key engineering strategies, including cofactor regeneration, pathway balancing, and semicontinuous operation, to enhance system performance. Furthermore, we highlight emerging opportunities to integrate CFPS with artificial intelligence-guided design, renewable feedstocks, and modular reactor technologies toward more sustainable and scalable biomanufacturing processes.

papers.title: On-demand biomanufacturing via programmed SporeBot.
papers.abstract: Biopharmaceuticals, including antimicrobial peptides and engineered protein-based vaccines, represent key products of the biotechnology sector. However, their reliance on large-scale manufacturing and cold-chain logistics limits deployment in field and resource-limited settings. To address this gap, we developed SporeBot, a platform that exploits the intrinsic stability of Bacillus subtilis spores for versatile and on-demand biopharmaceutical production. The platform comprises polymeric microcapsules that encapsulate engineered spores. These spores exhibit robust stability, retaining engineered functionality under harsh conditions and extended storage. Upon activation, germinated cells secrete the target proteins, which diffuse across a polymeric mesh that physically separates the cellular factory from the secreted product. We validate this platform through the production and functional testing of antimicrobial peptides and vaccine antigens. Our approach resolves key manufacturing and distribution constraints of protein therapeutics and offers a deployable solution for on-demand biomanufacturing in both developed and resource-limited settings.

papers.title: Hierarchical design strategies for tuning genetic circuits.
papers.abstract: Genetic circuit design is central to synthetic biology, yet achieving predictable and programmable circuit performance remains challenging due to diverse circuit- and host-dependent factors. Thus, a systematic perspective is needed to integrate these factors across multiple design layers. In this review, we establish a hierarchical framework for tuning genetic circuits as an engineering process spanning biological part design, DNA synthesis and assembly, carrier selection, host-cell implementation, and cross-host transfer. We further discuss how each layer contributes to circuit behavior and shapes trade-offs among key performance properties. By integrating hierarchical design strategies with iterative troubleshooting, this review provides a practical roadmap for tuning genetic circuits toward more predictable and reliable performance.

papers.title: Efficient Bioproduction of Citric Acid in Aspergillus niger.
papers.abstract: Citric acid is the most widely produced organic acid in industrial biotechnology, with a global annual output exceeding 2 million tons and broad applications across the food, pharmaceutical, chemical, and environmental sectors. Despite more than a century of industrial development since the discovery of citric acid fermentation by Aspergillus niger in 1917, current production systems are approaching critical bottlenecks in strain performance, process efficiency, and environmental sustainability. Increasing evidence indicates that citrate overproduction is not governed by a single metabolic pathway but emerges as a multi-constraint-driven systems phenomenon involving coordinated regulation of metabolism, cellular physiology, and environmental conditions. Recent advances in systems biology and synthetic biology have enabled a paradigm shift from empirical optimization to rational and programmable biomanufacturing. The integration of multi-omics data with genome-scale metabolic models has substantially deepened the understanding of citrate overflow metabolism. In parallel, the development of CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, dynamic gene regulation systems, and promoter engineering has enabled precise and multiplexed rewiring of metabolic networks. Targeted engineering strategies focusing on carbon uptake, mitochondrial metabolism, citrate transport, and morphology regulation have demonstrated that high-level production requires coordinated multi-layer optimization rather than single-gene modifications. At the process level, emerging strategies, including immobilized fermentation, in situ product recovery, and the utilization of alternative non-food feedstocks, are being increasingly integrated with engineered strains to enhance productivity and sustainability. These advances collectively point toward a transition from conventional fermentation to a multi-scale, integrated biomanufacturing framework. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent progress in citric acid biomanufacturing, covering the evolution of industrial A. niger strains, systems-level mechanisms of citrate accumulation, synthetic biology-enabled tool development, rational chassis engineering strategies, and process intensification approaches. Finally, we discuss future directions, including dynamic metabolic control, artificial intelligence-assisted design, and circular biorefinery systems, aiming to establish a fully integrated, intelligent, and sustainable paradigm for next-generation citric acid production.

papers.title: Targeting bacterial signaling pathways: a paradigm shift in antimicrobial strategies for food safety.
papers.abstract: Foodborne bacterial contamination represents a critical challenge to global food safety and public health. Pathogenic bacteria cause millions of foodborne illnesses annually, while spoilage organisms lead to substantial economic losses through product deterioration. Nearly one in ten people worldwide contract foodborne illnesses each year, resulting in approximately 420,000 deaths annually. US$ 110 billion is lost each year in productivity and medical expenses resulting from unsafe food in low and middle-income countries. Conventional preservation methods face limitations including quality degradation, residual toxicity, and growing consumer demand for clean-label solutions. Bacterial signaling pathways orchestrate virulence, biofilm formation, and stress adaptation, offering novel anti-virulence targets that preserve food quality while minimizing microbial hazards. This review systematically examines three major bacterial signaling pathways as novel targets for food antimicrobial strategies. Emerging intervention platforms are evaluated, including computational biology, nanotechnology, synthetic biology, natural QS inhibitors, and enzymatic degradation strategies, with emphasis on practical applications in cold chain, fermented foods, and meat products. Targeting signaling pathways demonstrates significant potential for controlling pathogens. Key challenges include signal molecule stability in food matrices, bioavailability optimization. Multi-target intervention strategies combining computational screening, natural inhibitors, and engineered delivery systems represent the most promising direction for next-generation food antimicrobials.

papers.title: Diffusion integrity testing of small-area sterilizing-grade membrane filters in single-use assemblies.
papers.abstract: Sterile filtration represents the final critical step in biomanufacturing, where a sterilizing-grade membrane filter removes microbial contamination from the drug product - making filter integrity verification essential. While bubble point and gas-liquid diffusion tests are established non-destructive methods for hydrophilic membranes, diffusion testing offers high sensitivity to small defects and operates at lower test pressures. However, applying diffusion testing to small-area filters integrated into closed single-use assemblies remains challenging because pressure changes measured by automated integrity testers can arise not only from membrane diffusion, but also from assembly-related effects such as gas-permeable tubing, upstream volume and thermal equilibration. For low-area devices, these background contributions can become comparable to or greater than the membrane signal, reducing test sensitivity and complicating interpretation. This work presents a practical method for implementing diffusion-based integrity testing of small-format sterilizing-grade filters in final sealed single-use assemblies. The approach quantifies assembly-specific background contribution and incorporates it into an adjusted diffusion specification, allowing membrane-specific diffusion to be resolved without altering the assembled system. By accounting for system-derived measurement noise, the method enables reliable end-user integrity assessment of closed assemblies that cannot be reconfigured to reduce upstream volume or replace high-permeability tubing materials.

papers.title: Biotechnology has outgrown the organism.
papers.abstract: Synthetic biology increasingly produces hybrid constructs that blur the boundaries of organism-based biosafety regulation. We propose using the term 'biological entity', defined by its capacity to interact meaningfully with biological systems or to facilitate biological processes, as an initial screening category before regulatory classification, enabling more coherent and proportionate oversight.

papers.title: Physiological, behavioral, and genetic factors that shape interactions in the plant growth-promoting maize rhizosphere synthetic community.
papers.abstract: Profiling microbiomes is an important way to understand the function and composition of communities in the wild, but natural microbiomes are often highly complex and often unamenable to experimentation to reveal cause-and-effect relationships. By using a small group of cultivable strains to represent those found in the wild, synthetic communities are one solution to this problem. Here we describe the ma ize r hizosphere s ynthetic c ommunity (MARSc), a genome-enabled 31-member bacterial community representative of the diversity found on the roots of maize grown in Iowa soils. This community is built around Pseudomonas putida KT2440, a model maize rhizosphere colonist and synthetic biology chassis. We characterized microbe-microbe interactions and biofilm formation of MARSc members in a variety of environmental contexts, finding that both behaviors are broadly controlled by nutrient levels. Genomic analysis and microbiome profiling of these organisms revealed that annotated biofilm genes (such as surface attachment and exopolysaccharide production) were significantly correlated with rhizosphere abundance, but neither trait correlated to in vitro biofilm formation. In vitro interaction assay findings were surprisingly consistent with co-correlations of rhizosphere abundance among MARSc members on roots. Finally, we found that when applied to the roots, MARSc can increase maize biomass (dry weight) by up to 40%-50% under varying nitrogen fertilization levels. Altogether, MARSc is a useful tool for identifying some of the factors influencing rhizosphere microbiome assembly and will be a strong foundation for further work in this area.IMPORTANCEThe microbiome surrounding the roots of plants can play an integral role in plant health and growth, and it is composed of thousands of species of microbes that are specific to the plant and environment it is grown in. However, due to this complexity, little is known about the means by which microbiomes form. In this study, we developed the maize rhizosphere synthetic community (MARSc) to gain a better understanding of the formation and function of microbiomes on the roots of plants. This consortium consists of 30 bacterial isolates plus Pseudomonas putida KT2440, a model maize root colonist. In this study, we investigated the interactions between these organisms, their genomes, cultural characteristics, and growth on the roots of maize. We show that MARSc increases maize growth under low nitrogen fertilizer, suggesting it will be a useful tool for identifying the mechanisms behind microbiome formation and plant growth promotion.

papers.title: kinGEMs: A robust and scalable framework for resource-constraint models through stochastic tuning of deep learning-predicted kinetic parameters.
papers.abstract: The construction of accurate enzyme-constrained genome-scale models (ecGEMs) remains a critical challenge in systems biology, limited by sparse kinetic data and the need for biologically meaningful representations. This work presents an integrated framework combining CPI-Pred, a deep learning model to predict kinetic parameters (kcat) from sequence and compound embeddings, with kinGEMs, a pipeline to incorporate these uncertainty-aware parameters into ecGEMs for metabolic optimization. By leveraging representations at multiple scales, the approach captures sequence, structure, and kinetic data to enhance model generalizability and accuracy. Rigorous benchmarking demonstrates the framework's capability to predict growth rates and fluxes that are consistent with experimental observations and measured proteome fractions, reduce median flux variability by several folds, and yield better-constrained metabolic models by explicitly accounting for the uncertainty inherent in ML-predicted kinetic parameters. kinGEMs successfully generated ecGEMs for 93 models spanning a phylogenetically diverse set of organisms including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, parasitic protists, fungi, and mammalian cell lines. These innovations breakdown the barrier to application of ecGEMs to non-model organisms and open new avenues for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology in more industrially relevant hosts.

papers.title: L-Threonine production from acetate by metabolically engineered Corynebacterium glutamicum using a pH-controlled fed-batch process.
papers.abstract: Acetate has a considerable potential as a non-food feedstock for microbial bioproduction, yet its use for amino acid production remains underexplored. Here, we developed a process for L-threonine production from acetate as the sole carbon source with Corynebacterium glutamicum by integrating rational, genome-based metabolic engineering with pH-coupled fed-batch cultivation. The engineered strain AT-3 carried five chromosomal mutations that alleviated feedback inhibition of key enzymes and redirected carbon flux toward the aspartate pathway. Substrate supply was controlled using a custom Visual Basic-based feeding script that automatically adjusted the acetic acid feed in response to online pH measurements. Robust process performance was maintained during a tenfold scale-up from 100-mL DASbox to 1-L DASGIP bioreactors. The optimized process achieved an L-threonine titer of 10.04 g/L and a yield of 0.086 g/g acetate. This study provides a basis for further studies on the development and improvement of acetate-based amino acid production process. KEY POINTS: • Plasmid-free C. glutamicum strains produce L-threonine in acetate minimal medium • pH-controlled acetic acid feed in bioreactors improved L-threonine production • Acetate-based production of feed amino acids avoids competition with human food.
papers.authors: Broschard P, Endt N, Wirtz A, Glitz C, Baumgart M, Bott M.

papers.title: Biomimetic Nanosystems as Emerging Catalysts for Translational Innovation in Healthcare.
papers.abstract: Biomimetic nanosystems are engineered platforms at the nanoscale range that emulate selected structural and compositional features to reproduce their advantageous interactions with the complex biological environments. These systems, inspired by the biological cell membrane(s), have emerged as a promising technology with a variety of biomedical applications. However, they are still in their early stage of clinical development. Biomimetic nanosystems may be produced by incorporating the desired nanoparticles into synthesized membrane(s). Such nanosystems exhibit greater immunocompatibility, immune evasion, and extended circulation times. Therefore, this study examines the latest advancements in the design and engineering of biomimetic nanosystems, focusing on membrane insertion/integration, hybridization, surface functionalization and modification, and metabolic engineering that could enhance the multifunctionality, hybrid membrane engineering, stimulus-responsive behavior, and scalability of these systems. The unique characteristics of these nanosystems have been investigated and applied in various fields, including medicine delivery, vaccine research, antidote(s) manufacturing, imaging, and sensing, which are critically discussed. Furthermore, this review has summarized the practical challenges related to translation, such as stability, reproducibility, functionality, regulatory complexity, and efficacy. This review also highlights both the opportunities and limitations of these emerging platforms and outlines key directions for the development of clinically relevant nanomedicine. As a result, this study serves as the foundation for future research into the multifunctional nanobiomimetic system.

papers.title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux.
papers.abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.

papers.title: AI-enhanced CRISPR-Cas9 therapeutics: Advances in precision, safety, and delivery.
papers.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has transformed biomedical research and is advancing toward clinical translation. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) offers improved precision in guide RNA design, off-target prediction, and delivery optimization. This review synthesizes recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 for medical applications, covering core mechanisms, engineered variants, base and prime editors, and therapeutic applications including CAR T-cell and CAR-NK engineering, genetic disorders, infectious diseases, and regenerative medicine. Delivery strategies are evaluated with emphasis on AI-driven optimization. AI applications are highlighted across deep learning architectures for guide RNA design, AI-designed nucleases such as OpenCRISPR-1, structure-guided and AI-assisted design of compact high-fidelity SaCas9 variants, reinforcement learning for pipeline optimization, and roles in CAR T-cell therapy and safety assessment. Safety challenges are examined, including off-target effects, chromosomal rearrangements, immunogenicity, and regulatory concerns. Future directions emphasize multi-scale modeling, explainable AI, clinical validation, and integration with synthetic biology, single-cell sequencing, organoids, and nanomaterials. The convergence of AI and CRISPR-Cas9 holds substantial potential for personalized medicine.

papers.title: Engineering all human milk oligosaccharide fucosidic linkages in planta.
papers.abstract: Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) are a component of breast milk which improve infant health outcomes by modulating immune responses, inhibiting pathogen adhesion, and promoting healthy gut microbiota. Although their effects are well-documented, few HMOs have been clinically or biochemically studied because only a handful of the simplest HMOs out of >200 species are currently possible to chemically synthesize or produce in microbes via metabolic engineering in microbial hosts. In contrast, plants are naturally adept at biosynthesizing a wide range of complex polysaccharides, and they have recently been established as a heterologous system for HMO production. However, much of the structural diversity of HMOs has not yet been reproduced in a plant, particularly fucosylations. Four fucosidic linkages can be found in fucosylated HMOs, but only Fucα1-2Gal has been biosynthesized in planta. Here, we screened bacterial fucosyltransferases using the model plant Nicotiana benthamiana to produce 3-fucosyllactose (Fucα1-3Glc), lacto-N-fucopentaose II (Fucα1-4GlcNAc), and lacto-N-fucopentaose III (Fucα1-3GlcNAc), demonstrating that all four fucosidic linkages can be made in planta. Just twelve glycosidic linkages make up all the HMOs found in breast milk, and our findings increase the number of linkages made in planta from seven to ten, greatly expanding the variety of HMOs accessible in a plant.

papers.title: Chloroplast genome engineering: Recent advances, pathways towards commercialization and future directions.
papers.abstract: Chloroplasts are ideal biofactories because thousands of transgene copies integrated into each plant cell to produce high levels of recombinant proteins and enzymes. Because chloroplast genomes are predominantly maternally inherited, transgenes are generally not transmitted via pollen. Nuclear genome engineering ushered in the GMO revolution for crop protection that mostly required lower levels of transgene expression. Higher level expression and biosafety through gene containment facilitate new applications of GM crops, including production of high-value biopharmaceuticals and enzymes. This review focuses on recent advances in this field, including the first FDA approval of biopharmaceuticals made in plant cells for evaluation in human clinical trials, topical or oral drug delivery, marker free edible plants by removal of antibiotic resistance genes and novel post-translational modifications required to produce functional human proteins. In addition, new tools are discussed to improve DNA delivery, vector free assembly, episomal or integration methods, enhancement of transgene expression through optimization of regulatory sequences, codons, targeted genome editing and other innovations in biomanufacturing. Topical drug delivery using plant cells incorporated into chewing gums to control oral viruses, pathogenic bacteria, or yeast and oral drug delivery with therapeutic proteins made in plant cells to treat diabetes, obesity and cardiopulmonary diseases currently advanced to human clinical trials are discussed. In addition, high-value industrial enzymes for launching new products or to confer valuable agronomic traits or enhance photosynthesis are discussed. Future perspectives section provides examples of biotechnology products anticipated to be launched in the next 3-5 years, with opportunities and anticipated challenges.
papers.authors: Fatima I, Daniell H.

papers.title: Cell culture tightrope: Balancing amino acids and dipeptides to optimize media formulation and biomanufacturing performance.
papers.abstract: High-quality cell culture media remain central to mammalian bioprocessing as industry produces increasingly complex molecules at higher cell densities under intensified processing conditions. Amino acids represent a critical class of media components, serving as building blocks for endogenous and recombinant proteins and also as key regulators of cellular metabolism. This requires delivery of amino acids at concentrations that challenge their stability and solubility limits. This review provides an overview of amino acid roles in cell culture and how to choose their optimal levels in media formulations, with a focus on Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells. Omics-assisted medium development strategies are described to characterize amino acid metabolism and minimize metabolic inefficiencies arising from amino acid degradation. Additionally, genetic engineering approaches aimed at introducing amino acid auxotrophies or removing metabolic bottlenecks are discussed as complementary strategies to improve cell culture performance. Understanding the physicochemical limitations associated with amino acid solubility becomes increasingly important in concentrated media formulations. Emerging in silico thermodynamic models that capture interactions between amino acids and other media components are highlighted as valuable tools for predicting solubility limits and guiding rational media formulation strategies. Dipeptides represent an increasingly attractive alternative to free amino acids due to improved solubility, stability, and process-enhancing properties. Consequently, this review summarizes key dipeptides, current knowledge of their uptake and metabolism, and the amino acid and dipeptide transporters and cleavage enzymes. Finally, the review emphasizes the importance of smart media design by integrating experiments with modeling approaches to enable efficient, robust, and sustainable biomanufacturing processes.

papers.title: Biomimetic Nanosystems as Emerging Catalysts for Translational Innovation in Healthcare.
papers.abstract: Biomimetic nanosystems are engineered platforms at the nanoscale range that emulate selected structural and compositional features to reproduce their advantageous interactions with the complex biological environments. These systems, inspired by the biological cell membrane(s), have emerged as a promising technology with a variety of biomedical applications. However, they are still in their early stage of clinical development. Biomimetic nanosystems may be produced by incorporating the desired nanoparticles into synthesized membrane(s). Such nanosystems exhibit greater immunocompatibility, immune evasion, and extended circulation times. Therefore, this study examines the latest advancements in the design and engineering of biomimetic nanosystems, focusing on membrane insertion/integration, hybridization, surface functionalization and modification, and metabolic engineering that could enhance the multifunctionality, hybrid membrane engineering, stimulus-responsive behavior, and scalability of these systems. The unique characteristics of these nanosystems have been investigated and applied in various fields, including medicine delivery, vaccine research, antidote(s) manufacturing, imaging, and sensing, which are critically discussed. Furthermore, this review has summarized the practical challenges related to translation, such as stability, reproducibility, functionality, regulatory complexity, and efficacy. This review also highlights both the opportunities and limitations of these emerging platforms and outlines key directions for the development of clinically relevant nanomedicine. As a result, this study serves as the foundation for future research into the multifunctional nanobiomimetic system.

papers.title: Engineering all human milk oligosaccharide fucosidic linkages in planta.
papers.abstract: Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) are a component of breast milk which improve infant health outcomes by modulating immune responses, inhibiting pathogen adhesion, and promoting healthy gut microbiota. Although their effects are well-documented, few HMOs have been clinically or biochemically studied because only a handful of the simplest HMOs out of >200 species are currently possible to chemically synthesize or produce in microbes via metabolic engineering in microbial hosts. In contrast, plants are naturally adept at biosynthesizing a wide range of complex polysaccharides, and they have recently been established as a heterologous system for HMO production. However, much of the structural diversity of HMOs has not yet been reproduced in a plant, particularly fucosylations. Four fucosidic linkages can be found in fucosylated HMOs, but only Fucα1-2Gal has been biosynthesized in planta. Here, we screened bacterial fucosyltransferases using the model plant Nicotiana benthamiana to produce 3-fucosyllactose (Fucα1-3Glc), lacto-N-fucopentaose II (Fucα1-4GlcNAc), and lacto-N-fucopentaose III (Fucα1-3GlcNAc), demonstrating that all four fucosidic linkages can be made in planta. Just twelve glycosidic linkages make up all the HMOs found in breast milk, and our findings increase the number of linkages made in planta from seven to ten, greatly expanding the variety of HMOs accessible in a plant.

papers.title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux.
papers.abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.

papers.title: Chloroplast genome engineering: Recent advances, pathways towards commercialization and future directions.
papers.abstract: Chloroplasts are ideal biofactories because thousands of transgene copies integrated into each plant cell to produce high levels of recombinant proteins and enzymes. Because chloroplast genomes are predominantly maternally inherited, transgenes are generally not transmitted via pollen. Nuclear genome engineering ushered in the GMO revolution for crop protection that mostly required lower levels of transgene expression. Higher level expression and biosafety through gene containment facilitate new applications of GM crops, including production of high-value biopharmaceuticals and enzymes. This review focuses on recent advances in this field, including the first FDA approval of biopharmaceuticals made in plant cells for evaluation in human clinical trials, topical or oral drug delivery, marker free edible plants by removal of antibiotic resistance genes and novel post-translational modifications required to produce functional human proteins. In addition, new tools are discussed to improve DNA delivery, vector free assembly, episomal or integration methods, enhancement of transgene expression through optimization of regulatory sequences, codons, targeted genome editing and other innovations in biomanufacturing. Topical drug delivery using plant cells incorporated into chewing gums to control oral viruses, pathogenic bacteria, or yeast and oral drug delivery with therapeutic proteins made in plant cells to treat diabetes, obesity and cardiopulmonary diseases currently advanced to human clinical trials are discussed. In addition, high-value industrial enzymes for launching new products or to confer valuable agronomic traits or enhance photosynthesis are discussed. Future perspectives section provides examples of biotechnology products anticipated to be launched in the next 3-5 years, with opportunities and anticipated challenges.

papers.title: Cell culture tightrope: Balancing amino acids and dipeptides to optimize media formulation and biomanufacturing performance.
papers.abstract: High-quality cell culture media remain central to mammalian bioprocessing as industry produces increasingly complex molecules at higher cell densities under intensified processing conditions. Amino acids represent a critical class of media components, serving as building blocks for endogenous and recombinant proteins and also as key regulators of cellular metabolism. This requires delivery of amino acids at concentrations that challenge their stability and solubility limits. This review provides an overview of amino acid roles in cell culture and how to choose their optimal levels in media formulations, with a focus on Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells. Omics-assisted medium development strategies are described to characterize amino acid metabolism and minimize metabolic inefficiencies arising from amino acid degradation. Additionally, genetic engineering approaches aimed at introducing amino acid auxotrophies or removing metabolic bottlenecks are discussed as complementary strategies to improve cell culture performance. Understanding the physicochemical limitations associated with amino acid solubility becomes increasingly important in concentrated media formulations. Emerging in silico thermodynamic models that capture interactions between amino acids and other media components are highlighted as valuable tools for predicting solubility limits and guiding rational media formulation strategies. Dipeptides represent an increasingly attractive alternative to free amino acids due to improved solubility, stability, and process-enhancing properties. Consequently, this review summarizes key dipeptides, current knowledge of their uptake and metabolism, and the amino acid and dipeptide transporters and cleavage enzymes. Finally, the review emphasizes the importance of smart media design by integrating experiments with modeling approaches to enable efficient, robust, and sustainable biomanufacturing processes.

papers.title: Global health security and smallpox: A strategic review of post-eradication biosafety and preparedness.
papers.abstract: The global biosecurity framework faces a potential critical transition driven by synthetic biology advancements and declining population-level immunity. This review evaluates smallpox as a central case study for contemporary pathogen governance and biopolitical preparedness. We analyze the convergence of two primary risks: the technical feasibility of de novo orthopoxvirus synthesis and the expanding immunity gap following the cessation of routine vaccination. The 2022 mpox resurgence is assessed as a sentinel event revealing strategic vulnerabilities in cross-protective immunity. Ultimately, this perspective argues that smallpox reemergence risk is not merely a technological byproduct, but a fundamental global governance crisis. To mitigate these threats, we propose a multidimensional framework integrated with One Health principles and transnational coordination. Maintaining strategic vigilance and institutional memory is presented as a critical political capacity for post-eradication health security.

papers.abstract: Biological warfare involves the deliberate use of microorganisms or toxins to cause disease and death in humans, animals, or plants, and has occurred across state warfare, bioterrorism, biocrime, and accidental laboratory release. Despite a substantial historical literature, many commonly cited events lack rigorous primary-source documentation, and secondary reviews frequently perpetuate unverified claims. This review applies explicit evidentiary criteria to distinguish well-documented incidents from contested allegations and unsubstantiated claims, using Carus's typology to categorize events by actor and intent. Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO CRD42024592724), we searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus up to April 4, 2024, supplemented by grey literature and expert consultation. Two reviewers applied predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria to title/abstract and full-text screening. A 3-tier evidentiary framework (well-documented, contested, and unsubstantiated), adapted from elements of ROBIS and PRISMA, was applied to 48 candidate events identified between pre-historic times and 2019, with adjudication by subject-matter experts. Quantitative analysis was restricted to the 19 well-documented events to anchor findings to corroborated evidence from primary archival sources, forensic investigations, and specialist scholarship. The 19 well-documented events caused at minimum 21,595 injuries and 10,079 deaths, comprising 17 deliberate uses (89.5%) and 2 major accidental releases (10.5%). Deliberate events comprised 6 biocrimes (31.6%), 5 acts of warfare (26.3%), 4 bioterrorist attacks (21.1%), and 2 State-sponsored acts (10.5%). Fourteen biological agents were employed across 31 agent instances. CDC Category B agents predominated (58.1%, n = 18), followed by Category A (35.5%, n = 11); 2 agents did not fit into the CDC classification (6.5%), and no Category C agents were identified. Bacillus anthracis was the most frequently used agent (22.6%, n = 7), followed by ricin (12.9%, n = 4) and Vibrio cholerae (9.7%, n = 3). The principal dispersal methods were contaminated food and beverages (29.2%, n = 7) and direct inoculation and infected animals or insect vectors (12.5%, n = 3), respectively. Events occurred across 9 countries, with the United States most frequently affected (31.6%, n = 6). Perpetrators originated from 10 countries, with the United States, United Kingdom, and Japan together accounting for over half of the well-documented events. Fewer than half of the events identified across the historical literature (n = 19; 39.6%) met the criteria for well-documented status, underscoring the need for consistent evidentiary standards in biosecurity research. Prevention, early detection, and rapid response, supported by ethical research oversight and open-source surveillance, are essential to mitigating these threats.

papers.title: Advancing Terpenoid Biosynthesis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae: Synthetic Biology Approaches for Efficient Longifolene Production.
papers.abstract: The sustainable microbial production of high-value terpenoids like longifolene represents a critical frontier in green manufacturing, yet it is often hindered by systemic metabolic inefficiencies in microbial hosts. To address this, we present a comprehensive systems metabolic engineering framework in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that integrates three complementary modules to overcome the key bottlenecks of enzyme catalysis, cofactor supply, and precursor availability. First, we enhanced the catalytic module by employing the RII dimerization/docking domain-RI anchoring disruptor (RIDD-RIAD) peptide-mediated enzyme assembly and structure-guided Pinus sylvestris longifolene synthase (psTPS) variant screening, `which improved whole-cell longifolene production under the tested conditions. Second, to resolve nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) cofactor imbalance, we engineered a dual-regeneration system by introducing an exogenous formate dehydrogenase (FDH) and simultaneously amplifying endogenous pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) flux. Third, we reprogrammed central carbon metabolism by integrating the non-oxidative glycolysis (NOG) pathway and deleting the transcriptional repressors DOS2 and YNR063W, and was associated with a larger steady-state cytosolic acetyl-CoA pool, the essential terpenoid precursor. This multi-pronged strategy culminated in a highly optimized strain that achieved a titer of 92.84 mg/L in shake-flask cultures. Critically, the process was successfully scaled to a 5 L bioreactor under fed-batch conditions, yielding 4181.51 mg/L total longifolene at 204 h (3484.79 mg/L extracellular and 696.72 mg/L cell-associated), the highest total titer among the microbial reports identified in Supplementary Table S4. Differences in product recovery and cultivation protocols limit direct process comparisons. Our work demonstrates that coordinated optimization of enzyme assembly, cofactor regeneration, and carbon-flow reprogramming can substantially improve longifolene biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae. This study provides a longifolene-focused case study for modular pathway optimization, while broader application of this strategy to other terpenoids or natural products will require further pathway-specific validation.

papers.title: Ca 2+ signature gates responsiveness to exogenous auxin in Arabidopsis roots.
papers.abstract: Plants must continually balance growth with arrest, especially under stress. Auxin signaling acts as a central regulatory hub in this process, yet the mechanisms that dynamically tune auxin signaling in real time remain unknown. Here, we use the light-gated, Ca 2+ -permeable Channelrhodopsin 2 variant XXM2.0 to optogenetically impose defined Ca 2+ signatures on Arabidopsis root cells. Repetitive light activation triggers cytosolic Ca 2+ signals that in turn suppress membrane depolarization and Ca 2+ transients triggered by exogenous auxin. Moreover, prolonged optogenetic Ca 2+ stimulation affects auxin-responsive transcriptional reprogramming. As phenotypic output, reversible inhibition of root growth by suppressing cell division and elongation is observed. We further identify a candidate CaM7-CNGC14 module that likely mediates Ca 2+ -dependent gating of responsiveness to exogenous auxin as well as Ca 2+ -dependent root growth inhibition. Our study thus introduces a synthetic biology approach to decompose calcium-auxin crosstalk in plant cells, and demonstrates that optogenetically imposed cytosolic Ca 2+ signals act as dynamic regulators of auxin susceptibility in roots.

papers.title: Bacillus-mediated selenium nanoparticle biosynthesis: reduction pathways, cellular processes, and applications.
papers.abstract: Selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) have attracted considerable interest due to their unique physicochemical properties, low toxicity compared with inorganic selenium (Se) compounds, and diverse biological activities. Microorganisms, particularly species of the genus Bacillus, represent efficient biological platforms for SeNP synthesis because of their tolerance to selenium oxyanions and their ability to reduce selenite Se (IV) to elemental selenium (Se0) under mild conditions. Selenate-reduction is relatively poorly understood in this genus, so the candidate selenate-reductase system proposed here is inferred from selenium-respiring organisms and has not been genetically confirmed in Bacillus. This review summarizes current knowledge on Bacillus-mediated SeNP biosynthesis with an emphasis on microbial selenium transformation, cellular responses, and biochemical processes involved in nanoparticle formation. The roles of redox-associated pathways, reducing equivalents, candidate enzymes, metabolites, and extracellular biomolecules in selenium reduction, nucleation, and stabilization are critically discussed, while highlighting the limitations of current mechanistic understanding and the need for further genetic validation. In addition, this review examines how bacterial strain characteristics and cultivation conditions influence SeNP properties, including particle size, surface chemistry, stability, and biological activity. The applications of Bacillus-derived SeNPs, including antimicrobial, antioxidant, anticancer, agricultural, and environmental applications, are discussed in relation to the nanoparticle characteristics and biological performance. Throughout the review, evidence is explicitly attributed to the relevant source system, distinguishing among Bacillus-derived, other microbial, chemically synthesized, plant-derived, and general SeNP literature. Current biomedical evidence for Bacillus-mediated SeNPs is based predominantly on in-vitro studies. Finally, emerging approaches for improving microbial SeNP production through strain selection, metabolic engineering, and process optimization are highlighted. This review provides an integrated perspective on Bacillus-mediated SeNP biosynthesis, identifies future research directions and offers insights for researchers in microbiology, bioprocess engineering, animal nutrition and agricultural biotechnology.

papers.title: Metabolic shuttles between mitochondria and plastids: Roles of key transporters in coordinating carbon-nitrogen metabolism.
papers.abstract: Carbon and nitrogen metabolism in plant cells is distributed across multiple organelles, requiring extensive metabolite exchange to coordinate growth, development and environmental responses. Mitochondria and plastids function as interconnected metabolic hubs linked through the transport of carbon skeletons, amino acids, organic acids, and redox equivalents across organellar membranes. These transport processes are essential for integrating energy conversion processes, nitrogen assimilation, and biosynthetic metabolism. In this review, we integrate current knowledge of mitochondrial and plastid envelope transporters that mediate carbon-nitrogen exchange between organelles, focusing on recent characterisation of transporters with confirmed substrates. We discuss how these transporters contribute to the coordination of cellular metabolism, highlight emerging concepts regarding their regulation and integration, and identify major knowledge gaps in our understanding of interorganellar metabolic communication. Understanding how these transport systems collectively shape carbon-nitrogen fluxes is essential for deciphering metabolic flexibility and guiding metabolic engineering strategies in plants.

papers.title: Green production of short-chain diols through microbial fermentation and bioconversion: Current advances, challenges, and future perspectives.
papers.abstract: Short-chain diols (C2-C5) are important platform chemicals used in polymers, textiles, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and specialty chemicals. Their conventional petrochemical production is associated with fossil-resource dependence and substantial energy requirements, motivating the development of bio-based alternatives. However, existing knowledge remains fragmented across individual diols, microbial hosts, metabolic pathways, and production technologies, limiting systematic assessment of their relative performance and industrial feasibility. This review addresses these gaps through a product-oriented comparative analysis of microbial production of ethylene glycol, propanediols, butanediols, and pentanediols. It examines metabolic pathway design, host engineering, renewable feedstock utilization, and fermentation strategies, highlighting how precursor availability, intermediate toxicity, redox balance, and cofactor requirements influence product yield, titer, and productivity. The review further evaluates downstream recovery options and their implications for purification costs, alongside reported techno-economic and life-cycle assessment findings. Particular attention is given to the challenges of comparing studies with different process conditions, economic assumptions, and environmental system boundaries. Finally, the review distinguishes comparatively mature bio-based production platforms from emerging pathways and identifies priorities for improving process integration, economic competitiveness, and environmental performance. This integrated perspective provides a basis for evaluating research progress and guiding the development of commercially viable and environmentally sustainable short-chain diol production systems.

papers.title: Metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for improved polyphosphate production
papers.abstract: Finite high-grade phosphate rock reserves and rising legislative demand for phosphorus recycling create a need for processes converting phosphorus-containing residual streams into valuable products. Microbial synthesis of inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) could complement its energy-intensive chemical manufacturing while enabling phosphorus recovery in a value-added product with applications ranging from food processing to flame retardants and fertilizer. After orthophosphate (Pi) starvation and refeeding, Saccharomyces cerevisiae naturally accumulates polyP as a cellular Pi reserve, but the current multistage process complicates industrial implementation. Here, we identified metabolic interventions that uncouple polyP accumulation from Pi starvation by systematic evaluation of 57 engineered S. cerevisiae CEN.PK113-7D strains. Constitutive activation of the PHO regulon produced the strongest increase in polyP, whereas disruption of inositol pyrophosphate synthesis, Pi import, or the vacuolar transporter chaperone complex impaired accumulation. This pattern indicates that efficient polyP accumulation depends on coordinated activation of Pi acquisition and vacuolar polymerization. Notably, deletion of PHO80 converted a transient starvation response into a constitutive production phenotype, enabling high polyP accumulation during growth. Optimization of the growth medium increased the polyP content further, and efficient use of the supplied Pi was demonstrated, while electron microscopy paired with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy supported increased vacuolar storage. During aerobic exponential fed-batch cultivation, pho80Δ simultaneously formed biomass and polyP, reaching a polyP content of 22.1% of cell dry weight and a titer of 8.2 g/L, both expressed as KPO3 equivalents. These findings establish S. cerevisiae pho80Δ as a promising platform for biological polyP production and phosphorus recovery.

papers.title: Combinatorial Tuning of Multigene Biosynthetic Pathways based on RNA Interference.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning the expression level of multigene pathways remains a major challenge in engineering eukaryotic microbial cell factories. Modifications to individual pathway genes and CRISPR-based approaches often require repeated genome reconstruction, large regulatory components, or complex guide-array assembly. Here, we developed a lightweight, post-transcriptional RNAi-based strategy that enables fine-tuning gene expression without iterative genome editing. Size-selected small-RNA sequencing and functional testing were used to identify endogenous Pol III promoters spanning graded transcriptional strengths in Schizochytrium sp. Combining promoter strength with multiple short hairpin RNA (shRNA) target positions expanded the accessible repression range and enabled high-resolution gene-dosage tuning. The RNAi-based combined regulation strategy was applied to the three-gene carotenoid pathway of Schizochytrium sp. and the nine-gene docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) pathway of Yarrowia lipolytica, significantly enhancing the product production in both hosts. Integration of RNAi screening and dosage optimization further identified and tuned bypass pathways, increasing the ratio of DHA to docosapentaenoic acid (DPA) by 4.50-fold versus wild type. These gains were maintained during 5-L fermentation and serial passaging. This work establishes a compact and scalable regulatory framework for engineering complex biosynthetic pathways in eukaryotic microbial hosts.
papers.authors: Zhang Z, Xu Y, Li Z, Du F, Ma W, Yang G, Sun X.

papers.title: Decoding the landscape in biomanufacturing of xylose: metabolic bottlenecks and computation-assisted strategies.
papers.abstract: As the second most abundant sugar in lignocellulose, xylose suffers from low utilization efficiency due to carbon catabolite repression and the scarcity of natural metabolic pathways. This bottleneck leads to the wastage of nearly 40% of available carbohydrate sources, undermining the economic competitiveness of biorefineries. Overcoming these metabolic barriers is essential for the transition toward large-scale, sustainable biomanufacturing. This review comprehensively summarizes the main pathways of xylose metabolism, with a particular focus on its major metabolic products, rate-limiting enzymes, cofactor preferences, feedback regulation, and compartmentalization. Special attention is given to the significance of modifying rate-limiting enzymes for enhancing carbon flux in the xylose metabolic pathway. The study aims to integrate current knowledge, and to provide support for further research. While enzyme limitations and redox imbalances persist, this review highlights how integrating AI-driven protein engineering with genome-scale metabolic models offers precise solutions. By optimizing key enzymes and correcting cofactor dependencies, these computational strategies provide a robust framework for overcoming metabolic bottlenecks. Ultimately, synergistic AI-metabolic modeling accelerates the efficient conversion of xylose, unlocking its transformative potential for the green bioeconomy.

This study provides a longifolene-focused case study for modular pathway optimization, while broader application of this strategy to other terpenoids or natural products will require further pathway-specific validation.

papers.abstract: The sustainable microbial production of high-value terpenoids like longifolene represents a critical frontier in green manufacturing, yet it is often hindered by systemic metabolic inefficiencies in microbial hosts. To address this, we present a comprehensive systems metabolic engineering framework in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that integrates three complementary modules to overcome the key bottlenecks of enzyme catalysis, cofactor supply, and precursor availability. First, we enhanced the catalytic module by employing the RII dimerization/docking domain-RI anchoring disruptor (RIDD-RIAD) peptide-mediated enzyme assembly and structure-guided Pinus sylvestris longifolene synthase (psTPS) variant screening, `which improved whole-cell longifolene production under the tested conditions. Second, to resolve nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) cofactor imbalance, we engineered a dual-regeneration system by introducing an exogenous formate dehydrogenase (FDH) and simultaneously amplifying endogenous pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) flux. Third, we reprogrammed central carbon metabolism by integrating the non-oxidative glycolysis (NOG) pathway and deleting the transcriptional repressors DOS2 and YNR063W, and was associated with a larger steady-state cytosolic acetyl-CoA pool, the essential terpenoid precursor. This multi-pronged strategy culminated in a highly optimized strain that achieved a titer of 92.84 mg/L in shake-flask cultures. Critically, the process was successfully scaled to a 5 L bioreactor under fed-batch conditions, yielding 4181.51 mg/L total longifolene at 204 h (3484.79 mg/L extracellular and 696.72 mg/L cell-associated), the highest total titer among the microbial reports identified in Supplementary Table S4. Differences in product recovery and cultivation protocols limit direct process comparisons. Our work demonstrates that coordinated optimization of enzyme assembly, cofactor regeneration, and carbon-flow reprogramming can substantially improve longifolene biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae. This study provides a longifolene-focused case study for modular pathway optimization, while broader application of this strategy to other terpenoids or natural products will require further pathway-specific validation.

papers.title: Ca 2+ signature gates responsiveness to exogenous auxin in Arabidopsis roots.
papers.abstract: Plants must continually balance growth with arrest, especially under stress. Auxin signaling acts as a central regulatory hub in this process, yet the mechanisms that dynamically tune auxin signaling in real time remain unknown. Here, we use the light-gated, Ca 2+ -permeable Channelrhodopsin 2 variant XXM2.0 to optogenetically impose defined Ca 2+ signatures on Arabidopsis root cells. Repetitive light activation triggers cytosolic Ca 2+ signals that in turn suppress membrane depolarization and Ca 2+ transients triggered by exogenous auxin. Moreover, prolonged optogenetic Ca 2+ stimulation affects auxin-responsive transcriptional reprogramming. As phenotypic output, reversible inhibition of root growth by suppressing cell division and elongation is observed. We further identify a candidate CaM7-CNGC14 module that likely mediates Ca 2+ -dependent gating of responsiveness to exogenous auxin as well as Ca 2+ -dependent root growth inhibition. Our study thus introduces a synthetic biology approach to decompose calcium-auxin crosstalk in plant cells, and demonstrates that optogenetically imposed cytosolic Ca 2+ signals act as dynamic regulators of auxin susceptibility in roots.

papers.title: Bacillus-mediated selenium nanoparticle biosynthesis: reduction pathways, cellular processes, and applications.
papers.abstract: Selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) have attracted considerable interest due to their unique physicochemical properties, low toxicity compared with inorganic selenium (Se) compounds, and diverse biological activities. Microorganisms, particularly species of the genus Bacillus, represent efficient biological platforms for SeNP synthesis because of their tolerance to selenium oxyanions and their ability to reduce selenite Se (IV) to elemental selenium (Se0) under mild conditions. Selenate-reduction is relatively poorly understood in this genus, so the candidate selenate-reductase system proposed here is inferred from selenium-respiring organisms and has not been genetically confirmed in Bacillus. This review summarizes current knowledge on Bacillus-mediated SeNP biosynthesis with an emphasis on microbial selenium transformation, cellular responses, and biochemical processes involved in nanoparticle formation. The roles of redox-associated pathways, reducing equivalents, candidate enzymes, metabolites, and extracellular biomolecules in selenium reduction, nucleation, and stabilization are critically discussed, while highlighting the limitations of current mechanistic understanding and the need for further genetic validation. In addition, this review examines how bacterial strain characteristics and cultivation conditions influence SeNP properties, including particle size, surface chemistry, stability, and biological activity. The applications of Bacillus-derived SeNPs, including antimicrobial, antioxidant, anticancer, agricultural, and environmental applications, are discussed in relation to the nanoparticle characteristics and biological performance. Throughout the review, evidence is explicitly attributed to the relevant source system, distinguishing among Bacillus-derived, other microbial, chemically synthesized, plant-derived, and general SeNP literature. Current biomedical evidence for Bacillus-mediated SeNPs is based predominantly on in-vitro studies. Finally, emerging approaches for improving microbial SeNP production through strain selection, metabolic engineering, and process optimization are highlighted. This review provides an integrated perspective on Bacillus-mediated SeNP biosynthesis, identifies future research directions and offers insights for researchers in microbiology, bioprocess engineering, animal nutrition and agricultural biotechnology.

papers.title: Metabolic shuttles between mitochondria and plastids: Roles of key transporters in coordinating carbon-nitrogen metabolism.
papers.abstract: Carbon and nitrogen metabolism in plant cells is distributed across multiple organelles, requiring extensive metabolite exchange to coordinate growth, development and environmental responses. Mitochondria and plastids function as interconnected metabolic hubs linked through the transport of carbon skeletons, amino acids, organic acids, and redox equivalents across organellar membranes. These transport processes are essential for integrating energy conversion processes, nitrogen assimilation, and biosynthetic metabolism. In this review, we integrate current knowledge of mitochondrial and plastid envelope transporters that mediate carbon-nitrogen exchange between organelles, focusing on recent characterisation of transporters with confirmed substrates. We discuss how these transporters contribute to the coordination of cellular metabolism, highlight emerging concepts regarding their regulation and integration, and identify major knowledge gaps in our understanding of interorganellar metabolic communication. Understanding how these transport systems collectively shape carbon-nitrogen fluxes is essential for deciphering metabolic flexibility and guiding metabolic engineering strategies in plants.
