papers.title: Green production of short-chain diols through microbial fermentation and bioconversion: Current advances, challenges, and future perspectives.
papers.abstract: Short-chain diols (C2-C5) are important platform chemicals used in polymers, textiles, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and specialty chemicals. Their conventional petrochemical production is associated with fossil-resource dependence and substantial energy requirements, motivating the development of bio-based alternatives. However, existing knowledge remains fragmented across individual diols, microbial hosts, metabolic pathways, and production technologies, limiting systematic assessment of their relative performance and industrial feasibility. This review addresses these gaps through a product-oriented comparative analysis of microbial production of ethylene glycol, propanediols, butanediols, and pentanediols. It examines metabolic pathway design, host engineering, renewable feedstock utilization, and fermentation strategies, highlighting how precursor availability, intermediate toxicity, redox balance, and cofactor requirements influence product yield, titer, and productivity. The review further evaluates downstream recovery options and their implications for purification costs, alongside reported techno-economic and life-cycle assessment findings. Particular attention is given to the challenges of comparing studies with different process conditions, economic assumptions, and environmental system boundaries. Finally, the review distinguishes comparatively mature bio-based production platforms from emerging pathways and identifies priorities for improving process integration, economic competitiveness, and environmental performance. This integrated perspective provides a basis for evaluating research progress and guiding the development of commercially viable and environmentally sustainable short-chain diol production systems.

papers.title: Metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for improved polyphosphate production
papers.abstract: Finite high-grade phosphate rock reserves and rising legislative demand for phosphorus recycling create a need for processes converting phosphorus-containing residual streams into valuable products. Microbial synthesis of inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) could complement its energy-intensive chemical manufacturing while enabling phosphorus recovery in a value-added product with applications ranging from food processing to flame retardants and fertilizer. After orthophosphate (Pi) starvation and refeeding, Saccharomyces cerevisiae naturally accumulates polyP as a cellular Pi reserve, but the current multistage process complicates industrial implementation. Here, we identified metabolic interventions that uncouple polyP accumulation from Pi starvation by systematic evaluation of 57 engineered S. cerevisiae CEN.PK113-7D strains. Constitutive activation of the PHO regulon produced the strongest increase in polyP, whereas disruption of inositol pyrophosphate synthesis, Pi import, or the vacuolar transporter chaperone complex impaired accumulation. This pattern indicates that efficient polyP accumulation depends on coordinated activation of Pi acquisition and vacuolar polymerization. Notably, deletion of PHO80 converted a transient starvation response into a constitutive production phenotype, enabling high polyP accumulation during growth. Optimization of the growth medium increased the polyP content further, and efficient use of the supplied Pi was demonstrated, while electron microscopy paired with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy supported increased vacuolar storage. During aerobic exponential fed-batch cultivation, pho80Δ simultaneously formed biomass and polyP, reaching a polyP content of 22.1% of cell dry weight and a titer of 8.2 g/L, both expressed as KPO3 equivalents. These findings establish S. cerevisiae pho80Δ as a promising platform for biological polyP production and phosphorus recovery.

papers.title: Combinatorial Tuning of Multigene Biosynthetic Pathways based on RNA Interference.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning the expression level of multigene pathways remains a major challenge in engineering eukaryotic microbial cell factories. Modifications to individual pathway genes and CRISPR-based approaches often require repeated genome reconstruction, large regulatory components, or complex guide-array assembly. Here, we developed a lightweight, post-transcriptional RNAi-based strategy that enables fine-tuning gene expression without iterative genome editing. Size-selected small-RNA sequencing and functional testing were used to identify endogenous Pol III promoters spanning graded transcriptional strengths in Schizochytrium sp. Combining promoter strength with multiple short hairpin RNA (shRNA) target positions expanded the accessible repression range and enabled high-resolution gene-dosage tuning. The RNAi-based combined regulation strategy was applied to the three-gene carotenoid pathway of Schizochytrium sp. and the nine-gene docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) pathway of Yarrowia lipolytica, significantly enhancing the product production in both hosts. Integration of RNAi screening and dosage optimization further identified and tuned bypass pathways, increasing the ratio of DHA to docosapentaenoic acid (DPA) by 4.50-fold versus wild type. These gains were maintained during 5-L fermentation and serial passaging. This work establishes a compact and scalable regulatory framework for engineering complex biosynthetic pathways in eukaryotic microbial hosts.

papers.title: Decoding the landscape in biomanufacturing of xylose: metabolic bottlenecks and computation-assisted strategies.
papers.abstract: As the second most abundant sugar in lignocellulose, xylose suffers from low utilization efficiency due to carbon catabolite repression and the scarcity of natural metabolic pathways. This bottleneck leads to the wastage of nearly 40% of available carbohydrate sources, undermining the economic competitiveness of biorefineries. Overcoming these metabolic barriers is essential for the transition toward large-scale, sustainable biomanufacturing. This review comprehensively summarizes the main pathways of xylose metabolism, with a particular focus on its major metabolic products, rate-limiting enzymes, cofactor preferences, feedback regulation, and compartmentalization. Special attention is given to the significance of modifying rate-limiting enzymes for enhancing carbon flux in the xylose metabolic pathway. The study aims to integrate current knowledge, and to provide support for further research. While enzyme limitations and redox imbalances persist, this review highlights how integrating AI-driven protein engineering with genome-scale metabolic models offers precise solutions. By optimizing key enzymes and correcting cofactor dependencies, these computational strategies provide a robust framework for overcoming metabolic bottlenecks. Ultimately, synergistic AI-metabolic modeling accelerates the efficient conversion of xylose, unlocking its transformative potential for the green bioeconomy.

papers.title: Global health security and smallpox: A strategic review of post-eradication biosafety and preparedness.
papers.abstract: The global biosecurity framework faces a potential critical transition driven by synthetic biology advancements and declining population-level immunity. This review evaluates smallpox as a central case study for contemporary pathogen governance and biopolitical preparedness. We analyze the convergence of two primary risks: the technical feasibility of de novo orthopoxvirus synthesis and the expanding immunity gap following the cessation of routine vaccination. The 2022 mpox resurgence is assessed as a sentinel event revealing strategic vulnerabilities in cross-protective immunity. Ultimately, this perspective argues that smallpox reemergence risk is not merely a technological byproduct, but a fundamental global governance crisis. To mitigate these threats, we propose a multidimensional framework integrated with One Health principles and transnational coordination. Maintaining strategic vigilance and institutional memory is presented as a critical political capacity for post-eradication health security.

papers.title: Biological Warfare, Bioterrorism, and Biocrime: A Systematic Review with Evidence-Based Historical Tiering (1763-2019).
papers.abstract: Biological warfare involves the deliberate use of microorganisms or toxins to cause disease and death in humans, animals, or plants, and has occurred across state warfare, bioterrorism, biocrime, and accidental laboratory release. Despite a substantial historical literature, many commonly cited events lack rigorous primary-source documentation, and secondary reviews frequently perpetuate unverified claims. This review applies explicit evidentiary criteria to distinguish well-documented incidents from contested allegations and unsubstantiated claims, using Carus's typology to categorize events by actor and intent. Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO CRD42024592724), we searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus up to April 4, 2024, supplemented by grey literature and expert consultation. Two reviewers applied predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria to title/abstract and full-text screening. A 3-tier evidentiary framework (well-documented, contested, and unsubstantiated), adapted from elements of ROBIS and PRISMA, was applied to 48 candidate events identified between pre-historic times and 2019, with adjudication by subject-matter experts. Quantitative analysis was restricted to the 19 well-documented events to anchor findings to corroborated evidence from primary archival sources, forensic investigations, and specialist scholarship. The 19 well-documented events caused at minimum 21,595 injuries and 10,079 deaths, comprising 17 deliberate uses (89.5%) and 2 major accidental releases (10.5%). Deliberate events comprised 6 biocrimes (31.6%), 5 acts of warfare (26.3%), 4 bioterrorist attacks (21.1%), and 2 State-sponsored acts (10.5%). Fourteen biological agents were employed across 31 agent instances. CDC Category B agents predominated (58.1%, n = 18), followed by Category A (35.5%, n = 11); 2 agents did not fit into the CDC classification (6.5%), and no Category C agents were identified. Bacillus anthracis was the most frequently used agent (22.6%, n = 7), followed by ricin (12.9%, n = 4) and Vibrio cholerae (9.7%, n = 3). The principal dispersal methods were contaminated food and beverages (29.2%, n = 7) and direct inoculation and infected animals or insect vectors (12.5%, n = 3), respectively. Events occurred across 9 countries, with the United States most frequently affected (31.6%, n = 6). Perpetrators originated from 10 countries, with the United States, United Kingdom, and Japan together accounting for over half of the well-documented events. Fewer than half of the events identified across the historical literature (n = 19; 39.6%) met the criteria for well-documented status, underscoring the need for consistent evidentiary standards in biosecurity research. Biological warfare remains a significant concern given its covert nature, the accessibility of low-technology dispersal methods, and emerging risks from synthetic biology, dual-use research, and artificial intelligence. Prevention, early detection, and rapid response, supported by ethical research oversight and open-source surveillance, are essential to mitigating these threats.

papers.title: Research progress in the production, purification, and applications of long single-stranded DNA.
papers.abstract: Long single-stranded DNA (long ssDNA) plays important roles in cutting-edge fields such as DNA origami, gene therapy, and synthetic biology. However, the production, preparation, and purification of long ssDNA remain technically challenging. This review systematically summarizes current strategies for long ssDNA production and preparation, including phage-E. coli-based biological production, template-dependent enzymatic amplification, and viral-vector-based generation of ssDNA genomes. CRISPR-Cas-assisted approaches are discussed separately as complementary tools for post-synthetic processing, sequence-selective cleavage, enrichment, and quality control, whereas other enzymatic approaches are considered for post-synthetic strand conversion. We compare the characteristics and limitations of these production and preparation strategies, discuss purification techniques for long ssDNA, and summarize its applications in DNA origami nanotechnology and gene therapy. This review comprehensively synthesizes the bottlenecks in long ssDNA production, preparation, and purification, and outlines further development trends. We highlight template-independent de novo enzymatic DNA synthesis, automated DNA manufacturing, synthetic biology-based production systems, and AI-assisted sequence optimization. These developments are expected to accelerate the transition of long ssDNA technologies from laboratory research toward scalable manufacturing and practical applications.

papers.title: Artificial photosynthetic cells: bridging chemical energization with biological functionalization.
papers.abstract: Artificial photosynthetic cells are nature-inspired systems that reproduce photosynthetic functions within cell/cell-mimetic compartments. Unlike discrete photocatalytic platforms, they integrate light harvesting, charge separation, multistep catalysis, selective transport, and compartmentalization to convert isolated photochemical reactions into coordinated cell-like functions. Driven by needs in carbon-neutral manufacturing, sustainable solar conversion, and precision medicine, the field is advancing from simple photocatalytic vesicles toward integrated and increasingly synthetic-cell platforms. In this review, we systematically elaborate on the rational design principles and emergent functional landscapes of artificial photosynthetic cells from a bioinspired perspective. We first decode the fundamental operational logic of natural photosynthesis, serving as a design blueprint. We then summarize the core construction modules of artificial photosynthetic cells, including cell-mimetic chassis, high-performance light-harvesting engines, multi-level catalytic networks, and precise interfacial engineering strategies. Furthermore, we categorize assembly paradigms into three mainstream branches: semi-artificial biohybrid systems, bottom-up reconstituted synthetic systems, and fully abiotic photosynthetic mimics. We further highlight a series of current and prospective functionalities, ranging from solar-driven CO 2 fixation and high-value chemical synthesis to in situ biomedical drug generation, as well as primitive life-like characteristics including intercellular communication, motility, and compartment division. Finally, we pinpoint the key technical bottlenecks, common pitfalls and outline opportunities enabled by the deep integration of synthetic biology, functional materials chemistry, and systematic bioengineering.

papers.title: Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has accelerated the design of structured proteins, but it remains difficult to design functional intrinsically disordered proteins because of weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function relationships1. papers.title: Biosensor-guided genome-wide CRISPR screens enable cis,cis-muconic acid overproduction in yeast
papers.abstract: Classical pathway metabolic engineering relies on enhancing strain productivity through the introduction of rationally identified genetic perturbations, which while useful, are time-consuming and miss unintuitive targets. Genome-wide CRISPR screens offer an alternative by efficiently sampling genomes, enabling the engineering of novel phenotypes, and are further enhanced when combined with high-throughput strain interrogation methods. Here, using Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we engineered small molecule biosensors into population enrichment tools using zeocin resistance and fluorescence as signal outputs. We then introduced the multi-functional genome-wide CRISPR (MAGIC) library that targets every gene for activation, interference, or deletion, thus creating biosensor-aided MAGIC, or senMAGIC. As a case study, we utilized senMAGIC to identify single genetic determinants that improve productivity of the nylon precursors protocatechuic and cis,cis-muconic acids (PCA and ccM). These were then randomly assembled as triple gRNA-tRNA arrays for multiplexed gene perturbations to identify combinatorial effects. Top gRNA hits were then confirmed using direct genomic integrations in senMAGIC-free production strains, resulting in identifying known as well as novel targets that increase PCA and ccM titres. Our results demonstrate senMAGIC as a robust automation-friendly whole-genome evolution tool and highlight limitations of the method, providing a roadmap for future multifunctional CRISPR screens to optimize host metabolism for efficient bioprocesses.

papers.title: Cyclotides from Clitoria ternatea: Genomic Organization, Biosynthesis, and Roles in Plant Defense.
papers.abstract: Clitoria ternatea, commonly known as butterfly pea, is a perennial legume widely recognized for its ornamental and medicinal value. Beyond its characteristic anthocyanin-rich blue flowers, the plant produces cyclotides, a type of ultra-stable, cyclic cystine-knot peptide, with exceptional biological functions. Unlike other cyclotide-bearing families that carry independent cyclotide genes, C. ternatea integrates cyclotide domains into albumin-1 genes, replacing β-chain domains through divergent or convergent evolution. Genomic and transcriptomic studies reveal a large repertoire of albumin-1 loci and associated biosynthetic enzymes, including asparaginyl endopeptidases (butelase-1), protein disulphide isomerases, and peptidyl-prolyl isomerases, which orchestrate the cyclization, folding, and stabilization of cyclotides. Transcriptome analyses further demonstrate tissue-specific expression patterns, with distinct cyclotides such as cliotides T2 and T3 enriched in flowers and pods, and cliotides T8-T10 specialized in seeds, reflecting adaptive responses to localized biotic stress. Functionally, C. ternatea cyclotides exhibit broad-spectrum defense properties, including insecticidal, bactericidal, nematicidal, and antifungal activities, primarily through membrane permeabilization and disruption of lipid bilayers. Their preferential affinity for phosphatidylethanolamine-rich membranes highlights their selective toxicity toward insect and microbial targets. Recent advances in synthetic biology exploit cyclotides' structural stability as molecular scaffolds for therapeutic peptide design, with applications in immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer drug development. This review consolidates genomic, transcriptomic, and functional insights into cyclotide biosynthesis and activity in C. ternatea, highlighting its evolutionary distinctiveness and biotechnological potential. Future research integrating multi-omics and spatial single-cell analyses can further unravel regulatory networks, defense dynamics, and translational applications of these unique plant peptides.

papers.title: Recent Advances in Microbial Community Composition of Fermented Soy Whey and Its Mechanism for Biotransformation of Soybean Isoflavones.
papers.abstract: Fermented soy whey (FSW), a traditional natural tofu coagulant, harbors complex microbial communities that drive soy-protein coagulation via organic-acid secretion and enhance the bioavailability of soybean isoflavones, conferring desirable flavor characteristics and health-beneficial bioactivities. However, several critical knowledge gaps restrict its scaled-up industrial deployment. The dynamic regulatory connections between microbial community temporal succession and metabolite biosynthesis during spontaneous FSW fermentation have not been fully deciphered. Interspecies interactions inside highly heterogeneous microbial consortia remain ambiguous, and the whole-fermentation system is exceptionally sensitive to fluctuating environmental conditions. This review synthesizes prior literature together with cutting-edge multi-omics datasets to systematically dissect the temporal dynamics of FSW microbial ecosystems. Enzymatic mechanistic analysis delineates key catalytic and metabolic pathways responsible for transforming soy isoflavone glucosides into aglycones and subsequent bioactive derivatives. We critically evaluate promising technical strategies, covering targeted synthetic-biology modification, integrated intelligent control systems, artificial intelligence, and digital-twin modeling, to advance the transition from experience-driven spontaneous fermentation to precision manufacturing. Selective manipulation of functional microbes or rate-limiting catalytic enzymes enables directional enrichment of high-activity isoflavone metabolites. This framework mitigates bioavailability drawbacks of native isoflavones and builds solid scientific foundations for zero-waste valorization of soy-processing by-products, circular food manufacturing, and innovative high-value-added functional-food development.

papers.title: N-GLYcanyzer monitoring of a microperfusion process reveals critical parameters' impact on Trastuzumab biosimilar N-glycoform time evolution
papers.abstract: Controlling monoclonal antibody (mAb) N-glycosylation as a critical quality attribute (CQA) remains challenging in continuous and intensified biomanufacturing, where conventional end-point analyses obscure dynamic pathway responses. Here, we deployed the N-GLYcanyzer process analytical technology (PAT) for automated monitoring of a microperfusion process that reveals critical parameters' impact on Trastuzumab biosimilar N-glycoform time evolution across a 20-day culture duration of Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cells in a ~2 mL scale-down microbioreactor perfusion platform. Using offline PAT assays combined with our integrated at-line PAT workflow, we systematically screened six perfusion process parameters: carbon source, viable cell density (VCD), perfusion rate, temperature, and pH. While nutrient limitation and thermal/acidic stress significantly disrupted N-glycans maturation, notably triggering high-mannose (Man5) accumulation and severe productivity penalties under pH 6.7 and 39 °C operation, targeted feed supplementation with galactose and MnCl 2 consistently shifted glycoform profiles away from G0F toward galactosylated species (G1F, G1F′, G2F). Crucially, coupling this combined feed strategy with an intensified perfusion rate (1.2 VVD) achieved a sustained, desired galactosylation shift without a productivity cost. papers.title: Beyond the Stool: Circulating Short-Chain Fatty Acids Better Predict Human Gut-Related Diseases.
papers.abstract: Background Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) mediate host-microbiota interactions and are typically measured in feces as markers of gut microbial activity. However, whether fecal SCFAs adequately reflect disease-associated host-microbiota dysfunction remains unclear. We hypothesized that circulating SCFAs, which integrate microbial production, intestinal absorption, barrier function, and host metabolism, provide a more informative representation of gut-related diseases. Methods Seven fecal and serum SCFAs were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry in 193 individuals, including patients with colorectal cancer (CRC, n = 30), celiac disease (CD, n = 35), obesity (OB, n = 33), and healthy controls (HCs, n = 95). We developed an interpretable machine-learning framework combining stacking ensembles, bootstrap validation, permutation testing, SHAP and LIME analyses. Cross-compartment predictive modeling was used to assess the reciprocal informativeness of fecal and circulating SCFAs. Results Circulating SCFAs exhibited markedly stronger disease-associated signatures than fecal SCFAs across all groups. Serum-based models achieved excellent classification performance (95% accuracy; multiclass ROC-AUC 1.00), whereas fecal SCFAs provided substantially lower predictive power (59% accuracy). Combining serum and fecal datasets yielded only marginal improvement (97.4% accuracy), indicating most diagnostic relevant information was already captured in circulation. Valeric, propionic, 2-methylbutyric, and isovaleric acids were consistently identified as the main contributors to disease discrimination. Cross-compartment modeling revealed weak predictive relationships between fecal and serum SCFAs, indicating these pools are largely non-redundant and reflect distinct biological processes. Conclusions Circulating SCFAs outperform fecal SCFAs as biomarkers of gut-related diseases, capturing the integrated effects of microbial activity and host physiology. These findings support blood-based SCFA profiling as a promising approach for precision diagnostics in microbiota-associated disorders.

papers.title: Fluidized Bed Cathodes Enable High-Rate CO2 to Formate Production and In Situ Microbial Growth
papers.abstract: Electrochemical CO2 Reduction Reaction (eCO2RR) to formate offers a sustainable and promising route for storing renewable electricity in a microbial energy substrate. Conventional CO2 electrolyzers rely on flat electrodes with limited catalytic surface area, mass-transfer constraints, and electrolytes that are incompatible with microbial growth, preventing direct coupling of electrochemical formate production with biological conversion. Here, we developed a biocompatible CO2 electrolysis configuration that uses fluidized particles of Sn, Bi, and In as electrocatalysts to enhance CO2 to formate conversion while supporting microbial utilization in the same chamber. The fluidized configuration enabled high formate production rates up to 0.24 mmol cm2 with Faradaic efficiencies of 86 to 92%, representing a two fold improvement over static electrodes. The system also achieved a carbon conversion efficiency of 42%, approaching the theoretical limit for co-generation of formate and bicarbonate. Importantly, electrolysis was performed in a biocompatible medium that supported direct in situ cultivation of Cupriavidus necator within the cathode chamber using only electricity and CO2/O2 as fed substrates. C. necator continuously consumed electro-generated formate for 5 to 6 days under aerobic conditions, demonstrating integrated CO2 to biomass conversion. This work establishes a fluidized electrocatalytic platform for simultaneous electrosynthesis and microbial upgrading in a single reactor, providing a scalable strategy for renewable carbon fixation and sustainable biomanufacturing.

papers.title: Engineering an Enzymatically Active Granular Matrix for On-Chip Modeling of Bone-Like Mineralization.
papers.abstract: Controlled biomineralization is central to engineering physiologically relevant hard-tissue models, yet achieving spatially organized, three-dimensional (3D) mineral deposition in microfluidic on-chip systems remains challenging. While cell-based bone-on-chip platforms offer biological complexity, they couple mineral initiation to matrix remodeling and paracrine signaling, complicating isolation of the earliest biochemical drivers of mineralization. Inspired by bottom-up synthetic biology, we engineered an enzymatically active granular matrix that recapitulates a key osteogenic function within a perfusable 3D microenvironment. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP), the key driver of native bone formation, was covalently conjugated to poly(ethylene glycol)-based (PEG) microgels via thiol-ene photochemistry, retaining over 90% of its initial activity after 24 h. These monodisperse microgels were assembled into a jammed, perfusable matrix on-chip, enabling independent control over enzyme loading and substrate delivery. The system supported in situ mineralization (24-48 h), yielding a calcium-deficient, poorly crystalline apatite-like phase characteristic of early-stage bone mineral. We demonstrate 3D localization of enzymatic activity to the granular matrix, which, coupled with interstitial perfusion, enabled mineral formation whose spatial distribution depended on the perfusion regime. This mechanistically defined, acellular platform provides a tunable foundation for investigating ALP-driven 3D mineralization and establishes a modular route toward hybrid biosynthetic models of (patho)physiological tissue mineralization.

papers.title: Arbitrium crosstalk enables shared signaling among phages.
papers.abstract: The arbitrium system has transformed our understanding of phage biology by demonstrating that temperate phages communicate through extracellular peptides to coordinate lysis-lysogeny decisions. Initially considered a highly specific signaling pathway restricted to individual phage lineages, arbitrium communication has now been shown to extend beyond lineage boundaries in some phage systems. Recent studies have shown that non-cognate arbitrium peptides can interact with heterologous receptors, providing evidence of inter-phage crosstalk. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of the molecular basis of arbitrium signaling, the structural determinants of peptide-receptor specificity, and the potential ecological and evolutionary consequences of inter-phage communication. We suggest that arbitrium crosstalk may shape phage ecology by mediating competitive and potentially cooperative interactions within shared signaling environments. We also discuss its potential uses in engineered phage systems, synthetic biology, and microbiome engineering. Collectively, the available evidence broadens the concept of viral communication beyond lineage-specific signaling, while the ecological significance and practical applications of arbitrium crosstalk remain to be established.

papers.title: Prokaryotes bridging the lipid divide.
papers.abstract: The fundamental biochemical and stereochemical difference in how cell membrane lipids are built between Archaea on one side, and Bacteria and Eukarya on the other is known as the lipid divide. It is often assumed to translate in the impossibility of combining membranes of both types. It was established early when little sampling of the biodiversity was available. Since then, exceptions have been revealed and accumulated. Here, we review those exceptions and complement them with a broad survey, revealing diverse bacteria with mixed membrane-lipid features. Together with liposome assays and synthetic-biology experiments, studies on these organisms suggest that the lipid divide can be bridged. We conclude by discussing the evolutionary implications for LUCA, the origin of the prokaryotic domains and eukaryogenesis.

papers.title: Functional Characterization and Application of Yarrowia lipolytica YlYxc1 for Enhanced Production of Sphingoid Bases.
papers.abstract: Long-chain bases (LCBs; sphingoid bases), derived from ceramide metabolism, are valuable sphingolipid intermediates for industrial applications. Here, we functionally characterized a putative ceramidase from Yarrowia lipolytica (YlYxc1) and evaluated its potential to enhance LCB production. YlYxc1 contains a conserved alkaline ceramidase motif with seven transmembrane helices and shares ~42% amino acid identity with Saccharomyces cerevisiae alkaline ceramidases ScYpc1 and ScYdc1. Despite lacking a canonical ER retention motif, YlYxc1 localized to the ER membrane. Deletion of YlYXC1 caused no major growth or lipid profile changes. Heterologous overexpression of YlYXC1 in S. cerevisiae wild-type and Scypc1Δydc1Δ strains increased phytosphingosine (PHS) production over dihydrosphingosine (DHS), mimicking ScYPC1 overexpression. In vitro activity assays using microsomal fractions from Scypc1Δydc1Δ cells expressing YlYXC1 revealed preferential hydrolysis of phytoceramide with an alkaline pH optimum. Furthermore, YlYXC1 expression in an engineered Y. lipolytica strain expressing heterologous acetyltransferases WcSLI1 and WcATF2 remarkably enhanced acetylated LCB production. Multi-copy integration of YlYXC1 into the Ylsur2Δsld1Δ strain also increased the secretory production of non-acetylated DHS. These findings establish YlYxc1 as a promising metabolic engineering target for producing value-added LCBs for pharmaceutical and cosmeceutical applications.

papers.title: Structure-guided engineering of medium- and long-chain triglycerides:​Fermentation-assisted biosynthesis, structural control and future perspective.
papers.abstract: Medium- and long-chain triglycerides (MLCTs) are triacylglycerols (TAGs) that have medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs) and long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) linked together on a single glycerol backbone. The positioning of the components, such as the MCFA-LCFA-MCFA (MLM-type) positioning, can affect lipase-mediated hydrolysis, release of fatty acids (FAs), absorption and metabolic behavior, however, structure-function relationships requires experimental validation. This review presents a comparison between chemical interesterification, lipase-catalyzed interesterification and fermentation-assisted biosynthesis of MLCT. Chemical interesterification will redistribute fatty acyl groups, but offers​ limited positional control, while lipase-catalyzed synthesis provides more positional selectivity but is susceptible to acyl migration. Fermentation-​assisted biosynthesis is a prospective approach that connects FA chain-length control, acyl-CoA supply and TAG assembly more strongly. However, there is currently more evidence that strongly supports the production of tailored FAs by microbes than demonstrated positional control of MLCT molecular species. Structural validation requires intact TAG molecular species analysis, positional analysis, and stereospecific analysis. An integrated framework combining applications of structural analysis, selective biocatalysis, fermentation optimization, metabolic engineering and functional evaluation is proposed.

papers.title: CultureBoost: an intelligent framework for retrospective analysis of commercial cell culture processes.
papers.abstract: Commercial-scale monoclonal antibody manufacturing requires stringent productivity control to maximize profitability. However, final productivity is frequently compromised by subtle process deviations beyond standard operating procedures, such as minor pH shifts, gas sparging variations, and nutrient consumption fluctuations. Although modern Industrial Internet of Things systems generate abundant inline and offline data, actionable process insights remain underexploited. To tackle the critical challenge of productivity fluctuations, identification of root causes is urgent. Therefore, this study proposes an intelligent retrospective data analysis framework for commercial-scale cell culture processes, integrating three core modules: inline data processing, offline data processing, and discriminative information extraction. It enables end-to-end automated historical data mining, quantifies factor contributions to batch quality variations, facilitates rapid potential root-cause identification with minimal data science expertise, and guides timely process optimization. Practical efficacy was demonstrated through two commercial-scale case studies manufacturing biosimilars to adalimumab (HS016) and trastuzumab (HS022), with data from over 30 batches collected per product. Critical factors possibly driving productivity declines were identified from early-batch data and successfully validated through targeted operational optimizations in subsequent runs. By converting latent process data into actionable insights, this scalable and operator-friendly framework provides a practical AI/ML-driven solution for continuous batch quality enhancement in GMP-regulated commercial biomanufacturing.

papers.title: Improving aerobic fermentation performance of glucose to gluconic acid production by cooperating with Gluconobacter oxydans and diatoms.
papers.abstract: Gluconic acid (GA) and its derivatives are widely demanded in construction, food and pharmaceutical industries. To mitigate food resource competition, the enzymatic hydrolysate of lignocellulosic agricultural waste (corncob) is regarded as a sustainable alternative feedstock for the GA bioproduction by Gluconobacter oxydans (G. oxydans). However, high‑solid hydrolysate causes dissolved‑oxygen deficiency due to increased broth viscosity, inhibiting the aerobic metabolism of this obligate aerobe. Herein, an economical diatom co‑cultivation system was constructed to supply oxygen in‑situ through photosynthesis. The neutralizer CaCO3 neutralizes GA and generates CO2 to partially sustain diatom photosynthesis, forming a chemically coupled interaction cycle (rather than strict mutualistic symbiosis). Experimental results demonstrated that diatom addition can effectively improve GA productivity. For corncob hydrolysate containing 100 g/L initial glucose, up to 32% higher GA yield was obtained. Such performance improvement is condition‑dependent, and limited enhancement was observed in high‑viscosity hydrolysate under high‑substrate loadings. This strategy partially mitigates oxygen‑transfer bottlenecks for lignocellulose‑derived GA production and provides a complementary low‑cost route for aerobic biomanufacturing of sugar acids from non‑food biomass.

papers.title: Arbitrium crosstalk enables shared signaling among phages.
papers.abstract: The arbitrium system has transformed our understanding of phage biology by demonstrating that temperate phages communicate through extracellular peptides to coordinate lysis-lysogeny decisions. Initially considered a highly specific signaling pathway restricted to individual phage lineages, arbitrium communication has now been shown to extend beyond lineage boundaries in some phage systems. Recent studies have shown that non-cognate arbitrium peptides can interact with heterologous receptors, providing evidence of inter-phage crosstalk. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of the molecular basis of arbitrium signaling, the structural determinants of peptide-receptor specificity, and the potential ecological and evolutionary consequences of inter-phage communication. We suggest that arbitrium crosstalk may shape phage ecology by mediating competitive and potentially cooperative interactions within shared signaling environments. We also discuss its potential uses in engineered phage systems, synthetic biology, and microbiome engineering. Collectively, the available evidence broadens the concept of viral communication beyond lineage-specific signaling, while the ecological significance and practical applications of arbitrium crosstalk remain to be established.

papers.title: Prokaryotes bridging the lipid divide.
papers.abstract: The fundamental biochemical and stereochemical difference in how cell membrane lipids are built between Archaea on one side, and Bacteria and Eukarya on the other is known as the lipid divide. It is often assumed to translate in the impossibility of combining membranes of both types. It was established early when little sampling of the biodiversity was available. Since then, exceptions have been revealed and accumulated. Here, we review those exceptions and complement them with a broad survey, revealing diverse bacteria with mixed membrane-lipid features. Together with liposome assays and synthetic-biology experiments, studies on these organisms suggest that the lipid divide can be bridged. We conclude by discussing the evolutionary implications for LUCA, the origin of the prokaryotic domains and eukaryogenesis.

papers.title: Recent Advances in Microbial Community Composition of Fermented Soy Whey and Its Mechanism for Biotransformation of Soybean Isoflavones.
papers.abstract: Fermented soy whey (FSW), a traditional natural tofu coagulant, harbors complex microbial communities that drive soy-protein coagulation via organic-acid secretion and enhance the bioavailability of soybean isoflavones, conferring desirable flavor characteristics and health-beneficial bioactivities. However, several critical knowledge gaps restrict its scaled-up industrial deployment. The dynamic regulatory connections between microbial community temporal succession and metabolite biosynthesis during spontaneous FSW fermentation have not been fully deciphered. Interspecies interactions inside highly heterogeneous microbial consortia remain ambiguous, and the whole-fermentation system is exceptionally sensitive to fluctuating environmental conditions. This review synthesizes prior literature together with cutting-edge multi-omics datasets to systematically dissect the temporal dynamics of FSW microbial ecosystems. Enzymatic mechanistic analysis delineates key catalytic and metabolic pathways responsible for transforming soy isoflavone glucosides into aglycones and subsequent bioactive derivatives. We critically evaluate promising technical strategies, covering targeted synthetic-biology modification, integrated intelligent control systems, artificial intelligence, and digital-twin modeling, to advance the transition from experience-driven spontaneous fermentation to precision manufacturing. Selective manipulation of functional microbes or rate-limiting catalytic enzymes enables directional enrichment of high-activity isoflavone metabolites. This framework mitigates bioavailability drawbacks of native isoflavones and builds solid scientific foundations for zero-waste valorization of soy-processing by-products, circular food manufacturing, and innovative high-value-added functional-food development.

papers.title: Functional Characterization and Application of Yarrowia lipolytica YlYxc1 for Enhanced Production of Sphingoid Bases.
papers.abstract: Long-chain bases (LCBs; sphingoid bases), derived from ceramide metabolism, are valuable sphingolipid intermediates for industrial applications. Here, we functionally characterized a putative ceramidase from Yarrowia lipolytica (YlYxc1) and evaluated its potential to enhance LCB production. YlYxc1 contains a conserved alkaline ceramidase motif with seven transmembrane helices and shares ~42% amino acid identity with Saccharomyces cerevisiae alkaline ceramidases ScYpc1 and ScYdc1. Despite lacking a canonical ER retention motif, YlYxc1 localized to the ER membrane. Deletion of YlYXC1 caused no major growth or lipid profile changes. Heterologous overexpression of YlYXC1 in S. cerevisiae wild-type and Scypc1Δydc1Δ strains increased phytosphingosine (PHS) production over dihydrosphingosine (DHS), mimicking ScYPC1 overexpression. In vitro activity assays using microsomal fractions from Scypc1Δydc1Δ cells expressing YlYXC1 revealed preferential hydrolysis of phytoceramide with an alkaline pH optimum. Furthermore, YlYXC1 expression in an engineered Y. lipolytica strain expressing heterologous acetyltransferases WcSLI1 and WcATF2 remarkably enhanced acetylated LCB production. Multi-copy integration of YlYXC1 into the Ylsur2Δsld1Δ strain also increased the secretory production of non-acetylated DHS. These findings establish YlYxc1 as a promising metabolic engineering target for producing value-added LCBs for pharmaceutical and cosmeceutical applications.

papers.title: Structure-guided engineering of medium- and long-chain triglycerides:​Fermentation-assisted biosynthesis, structural control and future perspective.
papers.abstract: Medium- and long-chain triglycerides (MLCTs) are triacylglycerols (TAGs) that have medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs) and long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) linked together on a single glycerol backbone. The positioning of the components, such as the MCFA-LCFA-MCFA (MLM-type) positioning, can affect lipase-mediated hydrolysis, release of fatty acids (FAs), absorption and metabolic behavior, however, structure-function relationships requires experimental validation. This review presents a comparison between chemical interesterification, lipase-catalyzed interesterification and fermentation-assisted biosynthesis of MLCT. Chemical interesterification will redistribute fatty acyl groups, but offers​ limited positional control, while lipase-catalyzed synthesis provides more positional selectivity but is susceptible to acyl migration. Fermentation-​assisted biosynthesis is a prospective approach that connects FA chain-length control, acyl-CoA supply and TAG assembly more strongly. However, there is currently more evidence that strongly supports the production of tailored FAs by microbes than demonstrated positional control of MLCT molecular species. Structural validation requires intact TAG molecular species analysis, positional analysis, and stereospecific analysis. An integrated framework combining applications of structural analysis, selective biocatalysis, fermentation optimization, metabolic engineering and functional evaluation is proposed.

papers.title: CultureBoost: an intelligent framework for retrospective analysis of commercial cell culture processes.
papers.abstract: Commercial-scale monoclonal antibody manufacturing requires stringent productivity control to maximize profitability. However, final productivity is frequently compromised by subtle process deviations beyond standard operating procedures, such as minor pH shifts, gas sparging variations, and nutrient consumption fluctuations. Although modern Industrial Internet of Things systems generate abundant inline and offline data, actionable process insights remain underexploited. To tackle the critical challenge of productivity fluctuations, identification of root causes is urgent. Therefore, this study proposes an intelligent retrospective data analysis framework for commercial-scale cell culture processes, integrating three core modules: inline data processing, offline data processing, and discriminative information extraction. It enables end-to-end automated historical data mining, quantifies factor contributions to batch quality variations, facilitates rapid potential root-cause identification with minimal data science expertise, and guides timely process optimization. Practical efficacy was demonstrated through two commercial-scale case studies manufacturing biosimilars to adalimumab (HS016) and trastuzumab (HS022), with data from over 30 batches collected per product. Critical factors possibly driving productivity declines were identified from early-batch data and successfully validated through targeted operational optimizations in subsequent runs. By converting latent process data into actionable insights, this scalable and operator-friendly framework provides a practical AI/ML-driven solution for continuous batch quality enhancement in GMP-regulated commercial biomanufacturing.

papers.title: Improving aerobic fermentation performance of glucose to gluconic acid production by cooperating with Gluconobacter oxydans and diatoms.
papers.abstract: Gluconic acid (GA) and its derivatives are widely demanded in construction, food and pharmaceutical industries. To mitigate food resource competition, the enzymatic hydrolysate of lignocellulosic agricultural waste (corncob) is regarded as a sustainable alternative feedstock for the GA bioproduction by Gluconobacter oxydans (G. oxydans). However, high‑solid hydrolysate causes dissolved‑oxygen deficiency due to increased broth viscosity, inhibiting the aerobic metabolism of this obligate aerobe. Herein, an economical diatom co‑cultivation system was constructed to supply oxygen in‑situ through photosynthesis. The neutralizer CaCO3 neutralizes GA and generates CO2 to partially sustain diatom photosynthesis, forming a chemically coupled interaction cycle (rather than strict mutualistic symbiosis). Experimental results demonstrated that diatom addition can effectively improve GA productivity. For corncob hydrolysate containing 100 g/L initial glucose, up to 32% higher GA yield was obtained. Such performance improvement is condition‑dependent, and limited enhancement was observed in high‑viscosity hydrolysate under high‑substrate loadings. This strategy partially mitigates oxygen‑transfer bottlenecks for lignocellulose‑derived GA production and provides a complementary low‑cost route for aerobic biomanufacturing of sugar acids from non‑food biomass.

papers.title: Expression of Human CYP2D6 in Artificial Cells Based on Polymer-Lipid Hybrid Vesicles.
papers.abstract: Artificial cells with the ability to express functional, biomedically relevant enzymes have long been a goal in the field of bottom-up synthetic biology. Here, we demonstrate the expression of human cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) within the lumen of giant hybrid vesicle-based artificial cells using a cell-free protein expression system based on the protozoan Leishmania tarentolae. The vesicle membranes comprise 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine and amphiphilic block copolymers containing poly(cholesteryl methacrylate-co-butyl methacrylate) with either poly(galactose methacrylate) (pGalacMA) or poly(carboxyethyl acrylate) as the hydrophilic block. The amount and composition of the block copolymer incorporated into the giant hybrid vesicle membrane altered the artificial cells' ability to support functional protein expression, likely through changes in membrane properties. In particular, giant hybrid vesicles containing pGalacMA supported production of enzymatically active CYP2D6. Overall, the reported approach advances the development of artificial cells capable of producing functional, biomedically relevant enzymes. Further, the effort highlights complex interplay between polymer properties and performance of biological components in the functional complexity achievable in polymer-lipid hybrid vesicles.

papers.title: Strain engineering of Aspergillus species for industrial enzymes bioproduction: a comprehensive review.
papers.abstract: Filamentous fungi of the genus Aspergillus, because of their exceptional secretory capacity and metabolic versatility have been extensively applied in traditional food fermentation and industrial biotechnology for production of diverse bioproducts. Their history of domestication and industrial application has enabled major progress in enzyme production; however, challenges associated with the filamentous growth and strain engineering for future biomanufacturing development still remain. This review summarizes the advances across the spectrum of strain-improvement methodologies, from classical mutagenesis, protoplast fusion, genome shuffling, and adaptive laboratory evolution to the modern era of CRISPR enabled genome editing, synthetic biology, and systems-level metabolic engineering. Previous reviews have primarily focused on individual Aspergillus species, specific industrial products or particular strain improvement approaches. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of classical and modern strain engineering technologies and industrial scale up across a wide range of Aspergillus species for industrial enzyme production. In particular, emerging non-GMO evolution tools such as atmospheric and room temperature plasma (ARTP) mutagenesis, and modern molecular biotechnology coupled with microdroplet-based ultrahigh-throughput screening, now allow the researchers to generate and screen a large number of Aspergillus species mutants with single-cell precision. The discovery of high-performance strains with enhanced secretion, stress tolerance, substrate utilization, and favorable enzymatic profiles for food and bioprocessing applications has been accelerated by the strain innovations. Collectively, these advances establish A. oryzae and the related species as increasingly reliable, scalable, and programmable hosts that can meet the biomanufacturing requirements of future circular and sustainable bioeconomies.

papers.title: Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling.
papers.abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin's protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin's retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose-response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.

papers.title: Yeast-Based Platforms for Next-Generation Human Health Applications.
papers.abstract: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

papers.title: Next-generation precision fermentation: integrating engineered cell factories, bioprocess intensification, and smart bioprocessing.
papers.abstract: Precision fermentation (PF) uses engineered microbial cell factories to manufacture defined products under controlled bioprocess conditions. In this review, PF is treated operationally as the integration of engineered hosts with metabolic engineering and process control, while traditional food fermentations without engineered production strains are excluded. The field now spans pharmaceuticals, food ingredients, industrial enzymes, specialty chemicals, and biopolymers, but commercial translation remains constrained by biological non-linearity, substrate and feedstock variability, mass-transfer limitations at scale, downstream recovery, and the cost gap with incumbent processes. This mini-review examines five connected layers: engineered microbial chassis; design build test learn (DBTL) and multi-omics-guided metabolic engineering; bioreactor intensification; Process Analytical Technology (PAT), soft sensors and AI-enabled control; and techno-economic and life cycle assessment. Quantitative case studies illustrate both the progress and the remaining scale-up gaps, including semi-synthetic artemisinin, recombinant insulin, lactic acid, succinic acid, QS-21, and polyhydroxyalkanoates. The central argument is that the next phase of PF will depend less on isolated improvements in strain performance than on coordinated integration of strain design, intensified operation, real-time process understanding, and rigorous economic and environmental assessment. This integration is essential for translating laboratory performance into reproducible, scalable, and commercially credible biomanufacturing. KEY POINTS: PF requires integration of cell-factory engineering with scalable bioprocessing rather than optimisation of any single layer. DBTL and multi-omics improve strain performance, but laboratory titres do not guarantee industrial scalability. Bioprocess intensification and real-time monitoring are required to convert strain performance into robust production. PAT, soft sensors, and AI strengthen process control when supported by reliable online data and qualified models. TEA and LCA should be integrated early to filter commercial and environmental feasibility before scale-up.

papers.title: Beyond Cell Factory: In Vitro Biotransformation (ivBT): A Paradigm-Shifting Biomanufacturing Platform.
papers.abstract: The paradigm of industrial biomanufacturing is shifting rapidly. Microbial fermentation mediated by cell factories is the dominant platform of biomanufacturing and has a history of thousands of years. However, their inherent properties, such as self-proliferation, cellular complexity, maintenance, and bioenergetic limits, could prevent them from being the best winner of biomanufacturing, especially for biocommodities and bioenergy. In this book chapter, we introduce a new concept of in vitro biotransformation (ivBT) as an emerging biomanufacturing platform that can surpass microbial cell factory. The development of ivBT is driven by the urgent great needs of food security and a new carbon-neutral energy society in the future. In theory, ivBT can have the theoretical yield and very high volumetric productivity and could have low-cost biomanufacturing costs. Furthermore, we highlight several representative applications, such as artificial photosynthesis for CO 2 -to-starch synthesis, in vitro respiration that can produce hydrogen under anaerobic conditions and electricity under aerobic conditions, directed glycosidic bond rearrangement (i.e., ATP-free or low-ATP biotransformation of cellulose to starch), and healthy sugars. Industrial biomanufacturing of myo-inositol, D-tagatose, and cellulosic starch would wipe off any prejudice (e.g., costly enzymes and short lifetime) and demonstrate transformative potential of ivBT. ivBT would be a paradigm-shifting biomanufacturing platform because it is like a dimensional reduction attack that can simplify extremely complicated cell factories by decreasing their dimensions.

papers.title: Valorizing watermelon rind waste into Plant-Based scaffolds for Proof-of-Concept cultivated meat production in a dynamic Fixed-Bed bioreactor.
papers.abstract: Cultivated meat (CM) biomanufacturing faces major challenges in cost and in scaling adherent-cell processes from the laboratory toward pilot and industrial production. This study presents a proof-of-concept (POC) in which watermelon rind, an agricultural waste by-product, was valorized into decellularized plant scaffolds (vDPS) and evaluated in a dynamic fixed-bed reactor (FBR). By replacing Triton® X-100 (1% v/v) with Tween-20 (10% v/v), we achieved effective decellularization, reducing residual DNA to below 25 ng/mg while eliminating the use of the toxic Triton X-100, making the scaffolds more suitable for CM applications. The resulting scaffolds exhibited high porosity (85.6%) and a Young's modulus of 36.8 ± 5.9 kPa, confirming their suitability for use as CM scaffolds. For dynamic bioreactor evaluation, the scaffolds were coated with Corning® Synthemax® II SC substrate and cultured with murine myoblast C2C12 cells under the process control capabilities of the Corning Ascent® fixed bed reactor (FBR) system. Over seven days, cells attached, proliferated, and differentiated; relative to static culture, the dynamic condition showed higher metabolic activity and denser cell coverage. Myogenic differentiation was confirmed by Myosin heavy chain and Desmin expression, and cross-sectional imaging showed cell penetration into the scaffold. The prototypes remained structurally stable after cooking. Overall, this work demonstrates the feasibility of integrating waste-valorized scaffolds into a dynamic FBR system, providing a POC foundation for future scale-up studies.
